lessons.title: A refusal, an alternative and a deferred answer
lessons.description: Follow a friend’s karaoke invitation through a real scheduling decision.
lessons.canDo: Distinguish a declined day from interest and a reply still pending

lessons.title: A formal no and a possibility with conditions
lessons.description: Follow a workshop capacity request through a refused option and a later written answer.
lessons.canDo: Separate inability, qualified possibility and a confirmed alternative

grammar.title: Hear a refusal in the complete exchange
grammar.formation: Invitation/request + ちょっと… or …はちょっと + a reason or following response. ちょっと also means a little in other contexts.
grammar.explanation: An unfinished response can soften a refusal. Here, Saturday is followed by an early departure and then an explicit decision not to go. That exchange supports the refusal; the word ちょっと alone does not. A speaker can state a limit directly and offer another day. Relationship and the particular request matter. Do not treat every brief answer as evasive or assign a hidden intention to every speaker.
grammar.example: 土曜はちょっと…。翌朝早いんだ。
grammar.translation: Saturday won’t really work… I have an early start the next morning.

examples.ja: {土曜|どよう}はちょっと…。{翌朝|よくあさ}{早|はや}いんだ。
examples.en: Saturday won’t really work… I have an early start the next morning.

examples.ja: その{時間|じかん}はちょっと{難|むずか}しいです。
examples.en: That time would be difficult.

examples.ja: {今|いま}はちょっと{手|て}が{離|はな}せない。{後|あと}でいい？
examples.en: I can’t stop what I’m doing right now. Would later be okay?

grammar.mistake: In ちょっと待って, the speaker asks for a brief wait. In a refusal, listen to the reason and following decision rather than memorising a hidden no.

grammar.title: A deferred answer is not a reservation
grammar.formation: 考えておきます / 考えておくね indicates consideration before a later occasion. Check a stated reply time or later acceptance/refusal.
grammar.explanation: The same phrase may postpone a real decision or close a conversation without a commitment. This lesson does not label it an automatic refusal. Yui promises to reply by Monday noon; Misaki waits before booking. An answer deadline is not proof that the invitation has been accepted. This retrieves earlier ておく preparation in a practical exchange.
grammar.example: 考えておくね。明日のお昼までに返事する。
grammar.translation: I’ll think about it and reply by noon tomorrow.

examples.ja: {考|かんが}えておくね。{明日|あした}のお{昼|ひる}までに{返事|へんじ}する。
examples.en: I’ll think about it and reply by noon tomorrow.

examples.ja: {考|かんが}えておきますが、{今|いま}はお{約束|やくそく}できません。
examples.en: I’ll consider it, but I can’t promise anything now.

examples.ja: {予定|よてい}を{確認|かくにん}してから、お{返事|へんじ}します。
examples.en: I’ll reply after checking my schedule.

grammar.mistake: Do not book on someone’s behalf because they said they would consider it. The later reply determines whether they can attend.

grammar.title: Formal inability is still a refusal
grammar.formation: Verb ます-stem + かねる / かねます: 引き受けかねます, 決めかねます. Not dictionary form + かねる.
grammar.explanation: This formal pattern states difficulty, inability or reluctance to carry out an action in the situation. お受けしかねます declines a request; it does not promise to try. 決めかねます says a decision cannot be made now. It is not a general replacement for every physical inability, such as not knowing how to swim. Distinguish stem + かねない, which can warn that something undesirable may happen; its meaning is different.
grammar.example: この条件ではお受けしかねます。
grammar.translation: We can’t accept those conditions.

examples.ja: この{条件|じょうけん}ではお{受|う}けしかねます。
examples.en: We can’t accept those conditions.

examples.ja: {今|いま}ここでは{決|き}めかねます。
examples.en: I can’t decide here and now.

examples.ja: その{方法|ほうほう}には{賛成|さんせい}しかねます。
examples.en: I can’t agree to that method.

grammar.mistake: The apparently affirmative かねます has a negative meaning. Do not turn かねません into a polite negative with the same meaning.

grammar.title: A double negative leaves limited room
grammar.formation: Verb plain negative + こともない (potential negative for ability); い-adjective negative + こともない; な-adjective + ではないこともない. Polite final ありません is possible.
grammar.explanation: A double negative allows some possibility without a strong yes. 行けないこともない means going is not wholly impossible, often followed by a limit. The related ないことはない can be similar; this is not a rigid particle-based certainty scale. In the workshop exchange, an afternoon option needs an instructor check. The reservation that follows matters more than a guessed yes/no from the first half.
grammar.example: 短い時間なら、手伝えないこともない。
grammar.translation: I could possibly help for a short time.

examples.ja: {短|みじか}い{時間|じかん}なら、{手伝|てつだ}えないこともない。
examples.en: I could possibly help for a short time.

examples.ja: {午後|ごご}だけなら{対応|たいおう}できないこともありませんが、{確認|かくにん}が{必要|ひつよう}です。
examples.en: An afternoon-only option may be possible, but we need to check.

examples.ja: {高|たか}くないこともないが、{毎日|まいにち}{使|つか}うなら{買|か}ってもいい。
examples.en: It is somewhat expensive, but I could buy it if I’ll use it every day.

grammar.mistake: 食べられないこともない permits limited ability; 食べられない denies it. Preserve the first negative and hear any following condition. Possibility is not acceptance.

dialogues.title: A karaoke invitation with a reply still pending

lines.speaker: Misaki
lines.line: {土曜|どよう}の{夜|よる}、カラオケ{行|い}かない？ {七時|しちじ}ぐらいから。
lines.romaji: Doyō no yoru, karaoke ikanai? Shichiji gurai kara.
lines.meaning: Want to go to karaoke Saturday evening? Around seven.

lines.speaker: Yui
lines.line: {土曜|どよう}はちょっと…。{日曜|にちよう}の{朝|あさ}、{名古屋|なごや}に{行|い}くんだ。
lines.romaji: Doyō wa chotto… Nichiyō no asa, Nagoya ni iku n da.
lines.meaning: Saturday won’t really work… I’m going to Nagoya Sunday morning.

lines.speaker: Misaki
lines.line: あ、{早|はや}いんだね。じゃあ、{日曜|にちよう}の{夜|よる}は？
lines.romaji: A, hayai n da ne. Jā, nichiyō no yoru wa?
lines.meaning: Oh, an early start. What about Sunday evening?

lines.speaker: Yui
lines.line: {帰|かえ}るのが{八時|はちじ}ごろだから、それも{無理|むり}かな。せっかく{誘|さそ}ってくれたのに、ごめん。
lines.romaji: Kaeru no ga hachiji goro da kara, sore mo muri kana. Sekkaku sasotte kureta no ni, gomen.
lines.meaning: I’ll get back around eight, so that won’t work either. Sorry, after you took the trouble to invite me.

lines.speaker: Misaki
lines.line: {大丈夫|だいじょうぶ}。{月曜|げつよう}ならどう？ {一時間|いちじかん}だけでも。
lines.romaji: Daijōbu. Getsuyō nara dō? Ichijikan dake demo.
lines.meaning: That’s okay. How about Monday, even just for an hour?

lines.speaker: Yui
lines.line: {月曜|げつよう}なら{行|い}けないこともないけど、{仕事|しごと}が{何時|なんじ}に{終|お}わるか、まだ{分|わ}からない。
lines.romaji: Getsuyō nara ikenai koto mo nai kedo, shigoto ga nanji ni owaru ka, mada wakaranai.
lines.meaning: Monday might be possible, but I don’t yet know when work will finish.

lines.speaker: Misaki
lines.line: そっか。{七時|しちじ}からにしようと{思|おも}ってるんだけど。
lines.romaji: Sokka. Shichiji kara ni shiyō to omotteru n da kedo.
lines.meaning: Okay. I was thinking of starting at seven.

lines.speaker: Yui
lines.line: {考|かんが}えておくね。{月曜|げつよう}のお{昼|ひる}までに{返事|へんじ}する。
lines.romaji: Kangaete oku ne. Getsuyō no ohiru made ni henji suru.
lines.meaning: I’ll think about it and reply by Monday noon.

lines.speaker: Misaki
lines.line: うん。じゃあ、{返事|へんじ}をもらってから{予約|よやく}するね。
lines.romaji: Un. Jā, henji o moratte kara yoyaku suru ne.
lines.meaning: Okay. I’ll book after I hear from you.

lines.speaker: Yui
lines.line: ありがとう。{土日|どにち}はやめておくけど、{月曜|げつよう}は{予定|よてい}を{確認|かくにん}してみる。
lines.romaji: Arigatō. Donichi wa yamete oku kedo, getsuyō wa yotei o kakunin shite miru.
lines.meaning: Thanks. I’ll skip the weekend, but I’ll check Monday’s schedule.

lines.speaker: Misaki
lines.line: {無理|むり}しなくていいよ。{別|べつ}の{日|ひ}もあるし。
lines.romaji: Muri shinakute ii yo. Betsu no hi mo aru shi.
lines.meaning: You don’t have to squeeze it in. We can go another day.

lines.speaker: Yui
lines.line: うん。{歌|うた}いたい{曲|きょく}はあるんだ。{今度|こんど}{聞|き}いてね。
lines.romaji: Un. Utaitai kyoku wa aru n da. Kondo kiite ne.
lines.meaning: Yeah. There’s a song I want to sing. Listen next time, okay?

dialogues.scene: Misaki invites Yui. They discuss dates without booking before Yui can answer.

dialogues.title: Forty participants and an afternoon option to check

lines.speaker: Tamura
lines.line: {来週|らいしゅう}{金曜|きんよう}の{研修|けんしゅう}ですが、{参加者|さんかしゃ}を{二十五名|にじゅうごめい}から{四十名|よんじゅうめい}に{増|ふ}やせますか。
lines.romaji: Raishū kin’yō no kenshū desu ga, sankasha o nijūgomei kara yonjūmei ni fuyasemasu ka.
lines.meaning: About next Friday’s workshop: can we increase the participants from twenty-five to forty?

lines.speaker: Ishikawa
lines.line: {申|もう}し{訳|わけ}ありませんが、{四十名|よんじゅうめい}ではお{受|う}けしかねます。{部屋|へや}は{三十名|さんじゅうめい}までです。
lines.romaji: Mōshiwake arimasen ga, yonjūmei de wa ouke shikanemasu. Heya wa sanjūmei made desu.
lines.meaning: I’m sorry, but we can’t accept forty. The room holds up to thirty.

lines.speaker: Tamura
lines.line: では、{午前|ごぜん}と{午後|ごご}に{二十名|にじゅうめい}ずつ{分|わ}けるのはどうでしょう。
lines.romaji: De wa, gozen to gogo ni nijūmei zutsu wakeru no wa dō deshō.
lines.meaning: How about splitting them into twenty in the morning and twenty in the afternoon?

lines.speaker: Ishikawa
lines.line: {午前|ごぜん}は{別|べつ}の{研修|けんしゅう}がありまして。{午後|ごご}だけなら{対応|たいおう}できないこともありませんが、{講師|こうし}の{予定|よてい}を{確認|かくにん}する{必要|ひつよう}があります。
lines.romaji: Gozen wa betsu no kenshū ga arimashite. Gogo dake nara taiō dekinai koto mo arimasen ga, kōshi no yotei o kakunin suru hitsuyō ga arimasu.
lines.meaning: There’s another workshop in the morning. An afternoon-only option may be possible, but we need to check the instructor’s schedule.

lines.speaker: Tamura
lines.line: {午後|ごご}に{二回|にかい}、ということですか。
lines.romaji: Gogo ni nikai, to iu koto desu ka.
lines.meaning: Do you mean two sessions in the afternoon?

lines.speaker: Ishikawa
lines.line: はい。ただ、{今|いま}ここでは{決|き}めかねます。{内容|ないよう}を{短|みじか}くできるか、{講師|こうし}にも{相談|そうだん}します。
lines.romaji: Hai. Tada, ima koko de wa kimekanemasu. Naiyō o mijikaku dekiru ka, kōshi ni mo sōdan shimasu.
lines.meaning: Yes. But I can’t decide here and now. I’ll also ask the instructor whether the material can be shortened.

lines.speaker: Tamura
lines.line: {分|わ}かりました。いつごろお{返事|へんじ}をいただけますか。
lines.romaji: Wakarimashita. Itsu goro ohenji o itadakemasu ka.
lines.meaning: Understood. When could we expect an answer?

lines.speaker: Ishikawa
lines.line: {水曜|すいよう}の{三時|さんじ}までに、メールでお{返事|へんじ}いたします。
lines.romaji: Suiyō no sanji made ni, mēru de ohenji itashimasu.
lines.meaning: I’ll reply by email by three on Wednesday.

lines.speaker: Tamura
lines.line: ありがとうございます。{返事|へんじ}をいただくまでは、{四十名|よんじゅうめい}に{案内|あんない}を{送|おく}らないようにします。
lines.romaji: Arigatō gozaimasu. Henji o itadaku made wa, yonjūmei ni annai o okuranai yō ni shimasu.
lines.meaning: Thank you. We won’t send invitations to all forty before your reply.

lines.speaker: Ishikawa
lines.line: お{手数|てすう}をおかけします。{難|むずか}しい{場合|ばあい}は、{別|べつ}の{日程|にってい}もご{提案|ていあん}します。
lines.romaji: Otesū o okake shimasu. Muzukashii baai wa, betsu no nittei mo goteian shimasu.
lines.meaning: Sorry for the trouble. If it won’t work, I’ll suggest another date.

lines.speaker: Tamura
lines.line: では、まずご{連絡|れんらく}をお{待|ま}ちします。
lines.romaji: De wa, mazu gorenraku o omachi shimasu.
lines.meaning: Then we’ll wait for your reply first.

lines.speaker: Ishikawa
lines.line: ありがとうございます。{二十五名|にじゅうごめい}での{現在|げんざい}の{予約|よやく}は、そのままにしておきます。
lines.romaji: Arigatō gozaimasu. Nijūgomei de no genzai no yoyaku wa, sono mama ni shite okimasu.
lines.meaning: Thank you. I’ll leave the current booking for twenty-five in place.

grammar: 考えておく and a later answer
watch.prompt: Optionally replay an invitation or request from your own material. Identify the proposed action, the actual reply and any condition or promised follow-up. Check the following exchange rather than guessing a hidden no from one phrase.

recycling.reason: The workshop naturally retrieves お手数 and 返信 from the recent email unit; older date, invitation and reservation vocabulary is also used. Genuine recent references cover 7.7 percent, so the target is explicitly seven percent. Supplementary recent conversation/committee headwords are not forced into these requests.

exercises.prompt: Which dates does Yui decline in this exchange?
exercises.explain: Yui’s later turn explicitly says she will skip both weekend days.

exercises.prompt: What is settled about Monday at the end of the call?
options: The room is booked for seven
Yui will reply by noon; attendance is not settled
Yui has agreed to sing for two hours
exercises.explain: The reply promise is explicit; Misaki will wait before booking.

exercises.prompt: Why would it be wrong to assume Yui dislikes singing?
options: She asks Misaki not to contact her again
She has already booked a solo room
She says there is a song she wants to sing
exercises.explain: The final turn expresses interest even though the schedule is not settled.

exercises.context: Form practice: complete the softened refusal with the short hedge taught here, before the stated early start.
exercises.explain: The following reason supports a refusal, while ぜひ/もちろん would express willing acceptance in this slot.
exercises.line: {土曜|どよう}は＿＿…。{翌朝|よくあさ}{早|はや}いんだ。

exercises.context: Misaki waits for an answer before booking. Complete the sequence, not a simultaneous action.
exercises.explain: てから places booking after receipt of the answer. The alternatives either wait during it or add an unsupported contrast.
exercises.line: {返事|へんじ}をもらって＿＿{予約|よやく}するね。

exercises.context: You tell a close friend you cannot answer yet, and will reply by noon tomorrow. Which whole reply fits?
options: {明日|あした}は{必|かなら}ず{行|い}く。{今|いま}{予約|よやく}して。
その{時間|じかん}は{絶対|ぜったい}{無理|むり}です。もう{誘|さそ}わないでください。
{考|かんが}えておくね。{明日|あした}のお{昼|ひる}までに{返事|へんじ}する。
exercises.explain: The first defers the decision and states the promised reply time. The others promise attendance or refuse further invitations.

exercises.meaning: Constrained form practice: put receiving the answer first, then booking, ending with ね.
exercises.explain: Booking follows the answer; a consideration phrase has not reserved a seat.

exercises.prompt: Why does Yui decline Monday in her actual reply?
exercises.explain: She distinguishes the changed work time from her tiredness after Sunday’s trip.

exercises.prompt: Which new plan was agreed in the phone call mentioned in the message?
options: Monday at seven for two hours
Wednesday at seven for one hour
exercises.explain: The second paragraph explicitly records Wednesday, seven and one hour.

exercises.prompt: What will they do if the karaoke room is unavailable?
options: Look for a faraway karaoke shop
exercises.explain: The message states an agreed nearby café fallback.

exercises.prompt: Which request is refused immediately?
options: Having forty people in the room together
exercises.explain: The room’s thirty-person limit rules out forty together.

exercises.prompt: Why is an afternoon alternative not confirmed during the call?
options: The client has already withdrawn every booking
The instructor’s schedule and shorter format need checking
exercises.explain: The following clauses specify two checks; the conditional possibility is not a confirmation.

exercises.prompt: When and how will Ishikawa answer?
options: By phone after next Friday’s workshop
Only if Tamura first invites all forty
By email by three on Wednesday
exercises.explain: The deadline and email method are explicit.

exercises.context: Use the formal refusal pattern かねます with 引き受ける. Select its ます-stem.
exercises.explain: 引き受けます minus ます gives 引き受け. Dictionary/て forms do not attach to かねます here.
exercises.line: そのご{依頼|いらい}は＿＿かねます。

exercises.context: The speaker leaves a limited possibility, not a firm yes. Keep both negatives in the taught double-negative pattern.
exercises.explain: 手伝えないこともない denies total inability. The other endings do not form this pattern.
exercises.line: {短|みじか}い{時間|じかん}なら、{手伝|てつだ}え＿＿こともない。

exercises.context: A client asks for forty participants in one room that holds thirty. Decline that request politely without promising acceptance.
options: {四十名|よんじゅうめい}ですね。ぜひお{越|こ}しください。
{三十名|さんじゅうめい}の{部屋|へや}ですが、{全員|ぜんいん}{必|かなら}ず{入|はい}れます。
{申|もう}し{訳|わけ}ありませんが、{四十名|よんじゅうめい}ではお{受|う}けしかねます。
exercises.explain: The first politely refuses the impossible capacity request. The other replies promise acceptance despite the stated limit.

exercises.meaning: Constrained form practice: state the inability to decide now, link it with ので, then promise an answer after checking.
exercises.explain: The check precedes the answer; neither phrase accepts the request now.

exercises.prompt: What afternoon option is available after the instructor check?
options: Twenty at one and twenty at three, one hour each
All forty at one for two hours
Twenty in the morning and twenty at three
exercises.explain: The first paragraph specifies separate twenty-person sessions at one and three.

exercises.prompt: What action and deadline are needed to change the booking?
options: Send invitations to forty before replying
Reply requesting the alternative by Thursday noon
exercises.explain: The third paragraph makes the reply the trigger for changing the booking.

exercises.prompt: Which booking remains valid while the reply is pending?
exercises.explain: The email explicitly preserves the twenty-five-person reservation; silence is not consent to a change.

lessons.title: A thought, a recollection and a narrative turn
lessons.description: Read an old bookmark and distinguish a remembered promise from the day’s outcome.
lessons.canDo: Follow event order and identify whose thought or recollection is narrated

lessons.title: Movement through a changing familiar place
lessons.description: Follow a remembered bakery, a real bookshop and a walk back through the alley.
lessons.canDo: Track perception, movement and decisions from a character’s viewpoint

grammar.title: Follow events before interpreting a tense switch
grammar.formation: Past narrative often uses …た / …ていた. Relative time comes from phrases such as その前, そのとき, 翌朝 and the sequence of events.
grammar.explanation: A story may recount completed events, describe the state around them and briefly show a scene as it appears to a character. A non-past sentence within a past story does not automatically announce a new present-day event. Follow the time expressions and viewpoint. This is reading practice with earlier forms, not a rule that every sentence in a novel must end in た.
grammar.example: 本を開いた。窓の外では雨が降っていた。
grammar.translation: She opened the book. Outside the window, it was raining.

examples.ja: {本|ほん}を{開|ひら}いた。{窓|まど}の{外|そと}では{雨|あめ}が{降|ふ}っていた。
examples.en: She opened the book. Outside the window, it was raining.

examples.ja: {前日|ぜんじつ}に{届|とど}いた{手紙|てがみ}を、その{朝|あさ}{読|よ}んだ。
examples.en: He read the letter that morning; it had arrived the previous day.

examples.ja: {角|かど}を{曲|ま}がった。{店|みせ}の{灯|あか}りが{見|み}える。{彼|かれ}は{足|あし}を{止|と}めた。
examples.en: He turned the corner. There was the shop’s light. He stopped.

grammar.mistake: The non-past 見える can bring the narrated scene into view. Do not move it to today without a time or viewpoint change in the text.

grammar.title: Identify the thinker, not just the quotation marks
grammar.formation: Plain clause + と + 思った / 思っていた. Noun / な-adjective predicates use だ before と; narration may name whose thought it is.
grammar.explanation: ユイは「もう遅い」と思った attributes a thought to Yui; it does not say she spoke aloud. Contrast 思った with 言った and a narrator’s description of what actually happened. A thought can later turn out to be mistaken. In a story, read the named person and surrounding sentences rather than treating every quotation as dialogue or every character’s belief as the outcome.
grammar.example: ユイは「もう遅い」と思ったが、店はまだ開いていた。
grammar.translation: Yui thought it was already too late, but the shop was still open.

examples.ja: ユイは「もう{遅|おそ}い」と{思|おも}ったが、{店|みせ}はまだ{開|あ}いていた。
examples.en: Yui thought it was already too late, but the shop was still open.

examples.ja: レンは「いい{名前|なまえ}だ」と{思|おも}った。
examples.en: Ren thought it was a good name.

examples.ja: 「また{来|こ}よう」と{心|こころ}の{中|なか}で{呟|つぶや}いた。
examples.en: “I’ll come back,” she said to herself silently.

grammar.mistake: 思った names the thinking event. The thought’s embedded verb need not match its past tense: 来ると思った can describe an expected arrival, not an arrival that already happened.

grammar.title: Recognise a narrator’s significant moment
grammar.formation: Plain clause + のだった. Noun / な-adjective non-past + なのだった; the preceding clause can itself be past or non-past.
grammar.explanation: In written narration, のだった may frame a background fact or give a moment significance within the story. It is not simply a mandatory past-tense version of んです. The preceding clause carries its own time, and context identifies why the narrator brings it forward. Here, a bookmark revives an old personal promise. Conversational んだった can instead recall a forgotten plan; do not give both uses one fixed English translation.
grammar.example: そこで初めて、自分の筆跡だと気づいたのだった。
grammar.translation: Only then did she realise it was her own handwriting.

examples.ja: そこで{初|はじ}めて、{自分|じぶん}の{筆跡|ひっせき}だと{気|き}づいたのだった。
examples.en: Only then did she realise it was her own handwriting.

examples.ja: {翌朝|よくあさ}には、この{町|まち}を{離|はな}れるのだった。
examples.en: The next morning, she would be leaving this town.

examples.ja: {十年前|じゅうねんまえ}、ここで{待|ま}つと{約束|やくそく}したのだった。
examples.en: Ten years earlier, she had promised to wait here.

grammar.mistake: Compare 去ったのだった, a departure already narrated, with 翌朝には去るのだった, a departure still ahead at that point. Read the clause and time phrase, not だった alone.

grammar.title: Track movement and change from the story’s viewpoint
grammar.formation: Verb て-form + くる / いく; past てきた / ていった. Physical direction and change over time depend on a reference point.
grammar.explanation: 近づいてきた presents an approach towards a viewpoint; 遠ざかっていった follows movement away. 明るくなってきた brings a developing change into view; 暗くなっていく follows its continuation. The reference point in a story can be a character at that moment, not the reader’s current location. Identify who perceives the change and which direction it takes. These are earlier constructions applied to narrative reading.
grammar.example: 路地の奥から笑い声が聞こえてきた。
grammar.translation: Laughter reached them from farther down the alley.

examples.ja: {路地|ろじ}の{奥|おく}から{笑|わら}い{声|ごえ}が{聞|き}こえてきた。
examples.en: Laughter reached them from farther down the alley.

examples.ja: {振|ふ}り{返|かえ}ると、{店|みせ}の{灯|あか}りが{遠|とお}ざかっていった。
examples.en: Looking back, he saw the shop’s light receding.

examples.ja: {読|よ}み{進|すす}めるうちに、{主人公|しゅじんこう}の{気持|きも}ちが{分|わ}かってきた。
examples.en: As she read on, she began to understand the main character’s feelings.

grammar.mistake: Do not translate every てくる as someone physically coming. The laughter and growing understanding describe perception or change.

grammar: ていく / てくる viewpoint
watch.prompt: Optionally select a short passage or scene from your own material. Mark one completed event, one thought and one change seen from a character’s position. Use later events to check what actually happened; save lines you want to reread.

recycling.reason: The café naturally retrieves 懐かしい/せっかく and the alley retrieves 笑い声 from recent units. Older books, rain, time and photographs fit these stories. The modest ten-percent recent-reference target avoids forcing formal phone or refusal vocabulary into a personal narrative.

exercises.prompt: Where was the blue bookmark when Ren found the book?
exercises.explain: Ren names page forty; the book had been at the back of the shelf.

exercises.prompt: What does Yui say about reading this book in university?
exercises.explain: She says she could not finish and had stopped at this point. She has not learned the continuation.

exercises.prompt: Why does Ren not hear the writing on the bookmark?
options: Yui is embarrassed and keeps it to herself
exercises.explain: Yui says she thinks the handwriting is hers and chooses not to read the embarrassing note aloud.

exercises.context: In the narrated background, the rain was already ongoing when she opened the book. Choose the past progressive.
exercises.line: {本|ほん}を{開|ひら}いたとき、{雨|あめ}が＿＿。
exercises.explain: 降っていた describes the ongoing background at the past opening; the others are a prediction and a request.

exercises.context: Use a complete noun-predicate quotation before と思った: she thought it was her own bookmark.
exercises.line: これは{自分|じぶん}の{栞|しおり}＿＿と{思|おも}った。
exercises.explain: In the explicitly complete quotation, the noun predicate uses だ before と. This task does not score casual omission as inherently wrong.

exercises.line: ユイは「また{読|よ}もう」と{心|こころ}の{中|なか}で{呟|つぶや}いた。
exercises.prompt: Who thinks these words, and are they spoken aloud?
options: Both; it is a public announcement
exercises.explain: ユイ is the thinker and 心の中で explicitly places the words in an inner monologue.

exercises.meaning: Constrained sequence: turn over the bookmark first, then read the small writing.
exercises.explain: 裏返してから fixes the event order: turning precedes reading.

exercises.prompt: Whose writing is eventually recognised on the bookmark?
exercises.explain: She recognises the handwriting and remembers writing it herself; the earlier friend-message thought is corrected.

exercises.prompt: What was the old promise?
options: Meet Ren at the sea that afternoon
Go to the sea after finishing the book
Send a letter before reading page forty
exercises.explain: The written condition is finishing the book. The narrator later identifies it as Yui’s promise to herself.

exercises.prompt: What has actually happened by the end of this episode?
options: She has finished the book and left for the sea
She has given the unread book to a stranger
She has read ten more pages and has not fixed a sea-trip date
exercises.explain: The bookmark moves from forty to fifty. The story remains unfinished, and she explicitly leaves the trip date undecided.

exercises.prompt: What is in the old bakery’s location now?
exercises.explain: The displayed books and Kenta’s reply establish that the premises are now a bookshop.

exercises.prompt: Why do they think they can still enter?
options: The shop is open all night
It is six thirty and the notice says seven
They have booked a morning visit
exercises.explain: Kenta reads today’s closing time and compares it with the current time.

exercises.prompt: What will Kenta do before photographing the old photo?
options: Phone his mother to close the shop
exercises.explain: The last line explicitly asks whether photographing it is allowed; permission has not yet been obtained in the scene.

exercises.context: From Kenta’s position, faint laughter begins to reach his ears from the alley. Choose the approach into perception.
exercises.line: {路地|ろじ}の{奥|おく}から{笑|わら}い{声|ごえ}が{聞|き}こえて＿＿。
exercises.explain: 聞こえてきた brings the sound into the perceiver’s awareness. No person must physically come.

exercises.context: They have left the shop. Looking back while walking away, he follows its light receding. Choose the continuation away.
exercises.line: {振|ふ}り{返|かえ}ると、{店|みせ}の{灯|あか}りが{遠|とお}ざかって＿＿。
exercises.explain: 遠ざかっていった follows recession away from the viewpoint, not an approach or benefit received.

exercises.line: ケンタはパン{屋|や}だと{思|おも}ったが、{窓|まど}には{本|ほん}が{並|なら}んでいた。
exercises.prompt: Which statement is supported by this sentence?
options: The shop still sells only bread
Misaki has said she dislikes books
Kenta initially thought it was a bakery, but books are displayed
exercises.explain: The thought is attributed to Kenta and contrasted with what is observed. It does not establish ongoing bread sales.

tiles: {一枚|いちまい}{撮|と}ってから
exercises.meaning: Constrained sequence: photograph it first, then leave the shop.
exercises.explain: 撮ってから orders the actions; it does not mean leaving before photographing.

exercises.prompt: What does Kenta recognise in the photograph?
options: Himself and his mother outside the old bakery
exercises.explain: The narrator explicitly says Kenta notices himself and his mother in the photo.

exercises.prompt: Which action has occurred, rather than merely being intended?
options: His mother has already received the photo
Kenta takes one photograph with permission
The bookshop has become a bakery again
exercises.explain: Taking a photo is narrated as completed; sending it tonight is a decision, with no later sending event shown.

exercises.prompt: At the end, why does the shop’s light recede?
options: The shop is moving towards them
They are still entering through the doorway
They are walking away and Kenta looks back
exercises.explain: They leave before seven and look back on their way home. The viewpoint follows their movement away.

lessons.title: An impression and the person’s explanation

grammar.title: An emotion suggested by what you see
grammar.formation: Established adjective stems + げ: 楽しい → 楽しげ; adjective + げな + noun / げに + verb.
grammar.explanation: げ describes an outward impression, often of emotion: 楽しげな声 is a voice that sounds happy. It does not prove the speaker’s feelings. Use established combinations such as 楽しげ, 寂しげ and 不安げ, rather than attaching it to every adjective. Usually the observer describes another person; context can also present other impressions. A guess can be corrected by the person’s own explanation.
grammar.example: ハナは楽しげに話している。
grammar.translation: Hana is talking with an air of enjoyment.

examples.ja: ハナは{楽|たの}しげに{話|はな}している。
examples.en: Hana is talking with an air of enjoyment.

examples.ja: {寂|さび}しげな{声|こえ}で「またね」と{言|い}った。
examples.en: She said “See you” in a lonely-sounding voice.

examples.ja: ユイは{不安|ふあん}げに{時計|とけい}を{見|み}た。
examples.en: Yui looked at the clock with an anxious air.

grammar.mistake: 楽しげに modifies the action; 楽しげな modifies a noun. Avoid a categorical claim that appearances reveal someone’s actual mood, or that any adjective freely takes げ.

grammar.title: A resemblance or a recurring trait
grammar.formation: Established noun / verb stem + っぽい; 忘れる → 忘れっぽい. Conjugates as an い-adjective: っぽくない / っぽかった.
grammar.explanation: 子供っぽい can describe a childish manner; 忘れっぽい describes a tendency to forget. The exact sense depends on the established combination. Many uses criticise a trait, but resemblance or colour need not be negative. Heat, watery taste and temperament are different contexts, not interchangeable symptoms. っぽい does not require that the person or thing is actually different from what it resembles.
grammar.example: ケンタは忘れっぽいので、メモを残す。
grammar.translation: Kenta leaves himself notes because he is forgetful.

examples.ja: ケンタは{忘|わす}れっぽいので、メモを{残|のこ}す。
examples.en: Kenta leaves himself notes because he is forgetful.

examples.ja: その{冗談|じょうだん}、ちょっと{子供|こども}っぽいね。
examples.en: That joke’s a little childish.

examples.ja: このスープは{水|みず}っぽくない。
examples.en: This soup isn’t watery.

grammar.mistake: Choose the word for the intended meaning. Do not substitute 忘れ気味 or 忘れがち everywhere: trait, current condition and recurrence can overlap, but their scope depends on context.

grammar.title: Ease of doing and a tendency to happen
grammar.formation: Verb ます-stem + やすい; 読みやすい / 読みやすくない. Contrast earlier にくい.
grammar.explanation: 読みやすい describes ease of reading; 緊張しやすい describes susceptibility to becoming tense. The verb and context determine which meaning fits. It is not the cheapness adjective 安い. 親しみやすい is a useful established expression for someone approachable. Readability, approachability and a likely reaction are distinct judgments, even though the same ending appears.
grammar.example: この筆跡は読みやすい。
grammar.translation: This handwriting is easy to read.

examples.ja: この{筆跡|ひっせき}は{読|よ}みやすい。
examples.en: This handwriting is easy to read.

examples.ja: ハナは{初対面|しょたいめん}の{人|ひと}の{前|まえ}で{緊張|きんちょう}しやすい。
examples.en: Hana tends to get nervous around people she’s just met.

examples.ja: {話|はなし}しかけやすい{雰囲気|ふんいき}だった。
examples.en: The atmosphere made it easy to start a conversation.

grammar.mistake: Ease belongs to the stated activity: 読みやすい is about reading, not necessarily writing. A tendency is not an inevitable outcome.

grammar.title: A recurring pattern, not just today
grammar.formation: Verb ます-stem / established noun + がち. Noun modification がちな / がちの; e.g. 遅れがちです.
grammar.explanation: がち marks something that tends to recur, often unwanted. 最近、返すのが遅れがち links it to repeated recent late returns. It is not a permanent identity or a count supplied by the suffix. The surrounding time expressions and examples establish the pattern. Use established combinations and distinguish one tired afternoon from several repeated incidents.
grammar.example: この二週間、返すのが遅れがちだ。
grammar.translation: Over these two weeks, I’ve tended to return things late.

examples.ja: この{二週間|にしゅうかん}、{返|かえ}すのが{遅|おく}れがちだ。
examples.en: Over these two weeks, I’ve tended to return things late.

examples.ja: {忙|いそが}しいと、{連絡|れんらく}を{忘|わす}れがちになる。
examples.en: When I’m busy, I tend to forget to get in touch.

examples.ja: {遠慮|えんりょ}がちなハナに、ユイが{声|こえ}をかけた。
examples.en: Yui spoke to Hana, who was hanging back a little.

grammar.mistake: Do not read がち as “always,” or infer a diagnosis or lifelong personality from repeated late returns.

grammar.title: A slight condition in the stated period
grammar.formation: Verb ます-stem / established noun + 気味（ぎみ）: 疲れ気味 / 寝不足気味. 気味の + noun; 気味だ / です.
grammar.explanation: 気味 describes a slight condition or developing tendency. 今週は寝不足気味 limits this case to this week; it need not be a repeated lifelong habit. In 疲れ気味, 気味 is pronounced ぎみ. The contrast with がち concerns the intended condition versus recurring pattern, not a universal rule that only the speaker can use 気味 or that it is restricted to health.
grammar.example: ケンタは今日、疲れ気味だ。
grammar.translation: Kenta is a bit tired today.

examples.ja: ケンタは{今日|きょう}、{疲|つか}れ{気味|ぎみ}だ。
examples.en: Kenta is a bit tired today.

examples.ja: {今週|こんしゅう}は{寝不足|ねぶそく}{気味|ぎみ}なんだ。
examples.en: I’ve been a little short of sleep this week.

examples.ja: レンは{緊張|きんちょう}{気味|ぎみ}の{声|こえ}で{挨拶|あいさつ}した。
examples.en: Ren greeted them in a slightly tense voice.

grammar.mistake: ぎみ is the suffix reading; standalone 気味 can have another reading and meaning. A tired-looking face alone does not prove someone has a fever.

watch.prompt: Optionally choose a short description or conversation from your own material. Identify one impression, one stated condition and one repeated action if present. Mark what the person actually explains; do not invent hidden feelings.

recycling.reason: The recent narrative unit naturally supplies a bookmark and handwriting in these scenes. A five-percent recent-reference target keeps the descriptions and library plan believable instead of importing unrelated formal refusal or business vocabulary.

exercises.prompt: What explanation did Yui hear from Mori-san himself?
options: He forgot his glasses and the print was hard to see
He had finished writing every note yesterday
exercises.explain: Yui reports his explanation about the glasses and print. She does not say he disliked the question.

exercises.prompt: How certain is Yui that the joke covered embarrassment?
options: She says Mori-san confirmed that reason
She suggests it as a possibility
She says there was no joke
exercises.explain: だったのかも marks Yui’s possible interpretation, not a confirmed statement by Mori-san.

exercises.prompt: Why does Mori-san say he writes things down?
options: He wants Hana to stop asking questions
exercises.explain: Yui explicitly attributes 忘れっぽいから何でも書く to Mori-san himself.

exercises.context: Complete the taught げ expression immediately before the noun 声: “a happy-sounding voice.”
exercises.line: {楽|たの}しげ＿＿{声|こえ}が{聞|き}こえた。
exercises.explain: The げ expression modifies the noun with な. に would modify an action, not 声 here.

exercises.context: Complete the taught げ expression immediately before the verb 言った: “said in a lonely-sounding manner.”
exercises.line: {寂|さび}しげ＿＿「またね」と{言|い}った。
exercises.explain: に links the manner to 言った. な attaches before a noun; ので would need the predicate connection and expresses a reason.

exercises.context: Use the ordinary present negative of 水っぽい, meaning “isn’t watery.”
exercises.line: このスープは{水|みず}っぽ＿＿。
exercises.explain: 水っぽい conjugates as an い-adjective: 水っぽくない. This is a formation task, not a choice among overlapping descriptions.

exercises.line: この{筆跡|ひっせき}は{読|よ}みやすい。
exercises.prompt: What is described as easy?
exercises.explain: The stem 読み identifies the activity as reading; writing is not stated.

exercises.prompt: What changes after Hana asks a question?
options: Mori-san refuses to speak to her
Mori-san answers calmly and explains the missing glasses
Hana learns Mori-san has banned questions
exercises.explain: The second paragraph narrates his calm answer, explanatory diagram and forgotten glasses.

exercises.prompt: What does Hana plan for the next encounter?
options: Claim she will never need to ask a question again
Prepare one question and ask directly
exercises.explain: The last paragraph chooses a prepared question, written down for the next encounter.

tiles: {真似|まね}するのは{難|むずか}しい
exercises.meaning: Constrained contrast: this handwriting is easy to read, but difficult to imitate.
exercises.explain: The contrast separates reading from imitating; it does not equate their difficulty.

exercises.prompt: Why does Kenta want to visit the library before the café?
options: His borrowed book is due today
His book was already returned yesterday
He wants to give the library his bookmark
exercises.explain: He says the return day is today and removes the bookmark rather than returning it.

exercises.prompt: What supports the recurring late-return pattern?
options: Only one tired afternoon with no late return
One day late last week and two days late the time before
A library notice saying every return is late
exercises.explain: Kenta gives two recent late returns. がち does not itself provide their counts.

exercises.prompt: What does Kenta take out before returning the book?
exercises.explain: 栞は抜いとこう states the removal. His next-book reminder is still a plan in the dialogue.

exercises.line: {今日|きょう}は{疲|つか}れ{気味|ぎみ}だ。
exercises.prompt: Which reading and meaning match the ending here?
options: ぎみ: a slight tired condition
きみ: you, the person addressed
exercises.explain: The suffix in 疲れ気味 is ぎみ and qualifies the tired condition; it does not mean always.

exercises.context: Use the taught verb-stem + がち pattern, with 遅れる, for repeatedly returning late.
exercises.line: {最近|さいきん}は{返|かえ}すのが＿＿がちだ。
exercises.explain: The ます-stem 遅れ attaches to がち. This task fixes the target pattern, rather than declaring 気味 or っぽい impossible in all contexts.

exercises.line: {今週|こんしゅう}は{寝不足|ねぶそく}{気味|ぎみ}だ。{最近|さいきん}は{返|かえ}すのが{遅|おく}れがちだ。
exercises.prompt: Which distinction follows from the wording?
options: A permanent illness and a rule that nobody returns books
Both sentences guarantee every return is late
This week’s sleep shortage and a recent recurring return pattern
exercises.explain: 今週 and 最近 locate the descriptions; slight shortage and recurrence are different scopes, not diagnoses or absolutes.

exercises.prompt: What is completed in the library note?
options: Today’s book is returned before the deadline
Every future book has been returned on time
The bookmark is donated to the library
exercises.explain: 今回は期限に間に合った records today’s return. The next due date is still two weeks away.

exercises.prompt: When does Kenta set a notification for the next return?

exercises.prompt: Where is the bookmark at the end?

exercises.meaning: Constrained completed sequence: returned the book, then went to the café.

lessons.title: A film’s source and the person who connected them

grammar.title: Name the material used to make a work
grammar.formation: Noun + をもとに（して） + predicate; noun + をもとにした + noun.
grammar.explanation: をもとに identifies source material used in making or developing something. A film may be made from old photographs or an interview. The phrase does not say the result copies every detail unchanged. をもとにした modifies a following noun. に基づいて can overlap in some contexts; this lesson tests the stated source and attachment, not a universal ban on other source expressions.
grammar.example: 古い写真をもとに映像を作った。
grammar.translation: They made the video using old photographs as source material.

examples.ja: {古|ふる}い{写真|しゃしん}をもとに{映像|えいぞう}を{作|つく}った。
examples.en: They made the video using old photographs as source material.

examples.ja: これは{実話|じつわ}をもとにした{脚本|きゃくほん}だ。
examples.en: This is a script based on a true story.

examples.ja: {聞|き}き{取|と}りの{記録|きろく}をもとに、{構成|こうせい}を{考|かんが}える。
examples.en: We’ll plan the structure from the interview record.

grammar.mistake: In this completed-work description, use をもとにした before the work’s noun. Do not substitute a dictionary-form modifier as if it carried the same completed relation. The source phrase alone does not prove historical accuracy.

grammar.title: Read a channel or the extent of a period
grammar.formation: Noun + を通じて（つうじて） / を通して（とおして） + predicate.
grammar.explanation: These expressions can name a channel or intermediary, or describe an extent such as a whole period. レンを通じて asks or arranges something through Ren; 一年を通じて describes the whole year. Many contexts also accept を通して. Preferences depend on wording and register; do not force a contrast that the context cannot support. A named intermediary is different from the material used to make a film.
grammar.example: レンを通じて、店主に話を聞いた。
grammar.translation: They interviewed the shop owner through Ren.

examples.ja: レンを{通|つう}じて、{店主|てんしゅ}に{話|はなし}を{聞|き}いた。
examples.en: They interviewed the shop owner through Ren.

examples.ja: {一年|いちねん}を{通|つう}じて、{商店街|しょうてんがい}を{撮影|さつえい}した。
examples.en: They filmed the shopping street throughout the year.

examples.ja: {交流|こうりゅう}を{通|とお}して、{違|ちが}う{世代|せだい}の{人|ひと}と{知|し}り{合|あ}った。
examples.en: Through the exchange, I got to know people of a different generation.

grammar.mistake: The readings つうじて and とおして match different written verbs. Both may be grammatical with periods or means; identify the role rather than guessing a uniquely permitted variant.

grammar.title: Follow the issue around which views differ
grammar.formation: Noun + をめぐって / をめぐり + predicate; noun + をめぐる + noun.
grammar.explanation: In a report, をめぐって presents an issue around which discussion or differing views develop. Here the cinema site’s future use is the shared issue. をめぐる modifies a noun, as in 跡地をめぐる議論. This is more marked and formal than an ordinary friend’s について; it belongs in the meeting report, not in every casual question. Disagreement does not itself tell you which proposal won.
grammar.example: 跡地の使い方をめぐって、意見が分かれた。
grammar.translation: Opinions differed over how to use the former site.

examples.ja: {跡地|あとち}の{使|つか}い{方|かた}をめぐって、{意見|いけん}が{分|わ}かれた。
examples.en: Opinions differed over how to use the former site.

examples.ja: {再開発|さいかいはつ}をめぐる{議論|ぎろん}が{続|つづ}いている。
examples.en: The debate over redevelopment is continuing.

examples.ja: {費用|ひよう}をめぐり、{二|ふた}つの{案|あん}を{比|くら}べた。
examples.en: They compared two proposals in a discussion centred on the cost.

grammar.mistake: Use をめぐる before 議論, not をめぐって議論 as a single noun modifier. A continuing discussion is not a completed decision.

grammar.title: Include a representative member of a wider group
grammar.formation: Noun + をはじめ（として） + clause; noun + をはじめとする + noun.
grammar.explanation: をはじめ names a prominent or representative member and includes others. 住民をはじめ、店主や学生も means residents as well as shop owners and students, not necessarily residents speaking first. をはじめとする connects to a following group noun. This phrase is common in formal speech and writing; this report lists who participated and then distinguishes their suggestions.
grammar.example: 住民をはじめ、店主や学生も参加した。
grammar.translation: Residents, as well as shop owners and students, took part.

examples.en: Residents, as well as shop owners and students, took part.

examples.ja: {資料館|しりょうかん}をはじめとする{施設|しせつ}が{協力|きょうりょく}した。

examples.en: Children and people from a wide range of generations enjoyed the film.

grammar.mistake: Do not infer chronological order from をはじめ. Before a noun use をはじめとする; before a clause をはじめ is possible.

grammar: channel or period: を通じて / を通して
issue: をめぐって / をめぐる
watch.prompt: Optionally use a short report or documentary from your own material. Identify the material or speaker behind one claim, an issue under discussion, and one proposal or decision. Save only expressions that actually occur; do not infer a speaking order from a participant list.

recycling.reason: The remembered bakery, familiar sign and alley naturally retrieve 見覚え and 路地 from the recent narrative unit. A five-percent recent-reference target preserves a believable screening conversation and report handover without padding with unrelated personality or refusal vocabulary.

exercises.prompt: What material did the makers use for the video?
exercises.explain: Misaki reports 古い写真をもとに作った. The film uses those photographs as material.

exercises.prompt: How did they get to interview the former shop owner?
options: By asking Mori at the meeting
Through Ren, whose mother knew the owner
By reading only the sign outside
exercises.explain: Misaki says レンを通じて and then explains the introduction through his mother’s friend.

exercises.prompt: What occupies the old bakery’s location now?
exercises.explain: Misaki identifies the place as the bookshop now. The cinema belongs to another scene.

exercises.context: Complete the taught をもとに expression immediately before 脚本: “a script based on a true story.”
exercises.line: {実話|じつわ}をもとに＿＿{脚本|きゃくほん}です。
exercises.explain: をもとにした modifies 脚本. をもとにして connects to a predicate; をもとにする脚本 would assign a different active role to the script.

exercises.line: {交流|こうりゅう}を{通|とお}して、{知|し}り{合|あ}った。
exercises.prompt: Which reading is written in this expression?
exercises.explain: 通して is とおして; 通じて would be つうじて. This tests reading, not a false grammatical prohibition on the other expression.

exercises.line: {一年|いちねん}を{通|つう}じて、{商店街|しょうてんがい}を{撮影|さつえい}した。
exercises.prompt: What role does 一年 play here?
options: The person who introduced the owner
The photographs used to make a script
The whole period over which filming took place
exercises.explain: 一年を通じて gives a period extending throughout the year. It is not an intermediary.

exercises.prompt: How long is the film shown at the venue?
exercises.explain: The first paragraph says 十二分の記録映画. A year is only the period in a separate grammar example.

exercises.prompt: How were the dates of the photographs checked?
options: By assuming every memory supplies an exact date
By asking about the vacant cinema site
exercises.explain: 写真の日付は資料館の記録で確かめた states the check. Memories are labelled separately.

exercises.prompt: What does the owner’s recorded narration bring across?
options: A decision to build parking at the cinema
A newly completed script for a fictional comedy
Smells and sounds not visible in the photographs
exercises.explain: The second paragraph names 匂いや音. The narration evokes them; photographs cannot literally reproduce smells.

exercises.meaning: Constrained source statement: made this video using old photographs.
exercises.explain: The source is the photographs; the made work is this video.

exercises.prompt: What was decided about the site’s final use?
options: It must all become a park
exercises.explain: Yui asks whether it is undecided, and Mori confirms they only shared proposals.

exercises.prompt: Which requests does Yui report?
options: People with children wanted parking; shop owners wanted a park
People with children wanted a park; shop owners wanted parking
Both groups wanted a new cinema
exercises.explain: Yui explicitly assigns the park and parking requests to those two groups.

exercises.prompt: What is the stated next step?
options: Check the dimensions and discuss it again next month
exercises.explain: The dimensions and alley entrance will be checked; the next meeting is next month.

exercises.context: Use the taught をめぐる noun-modifier pattern immediately before 議論: “debate over redevelopment.”
exercises.line: {再開発|さいかいはつ}を＿＿{議論|ぎろん}が{続|つづ}いている。
exercises.explain: をめぐる modifies the noun 議論. The other two connect the issue to a predicate, rather than forming this noun modifier.

exercises.context: Complete the taught をはじめとする pattern before 世代: generations including children.
exercises.line: {子供|こども}をはじめと＿＿{幅広|はばひろ}い{世代|せだい}が{集|あつ}まった。
exercises.explain: をはじめとする links the representative member to the group noun here. として and としながら do not form this modifier. The related past modifier とした is also possible in appropriate contexts, so it is not used as a wrong option.

exercises.line: {住民|じゅうみん}をはじめ、{店主|てんしゅ}や{学生|がくせい}も{参加|さんか}した。
exercises.prompt: What is stated about participation?
options: Residents took part, along with shop owners and students
exercises.explain: をはじめ includes other participants around the named representative group; it does not supply their speaking order.

exercises.prompt: Which additional proposal was offered?
options: Parking on the north side, with a park on the rest
Removing every tree for a new bookshop
exercises.explain: The third paragraph gives the north-side split as a proposal; its feasibility is still to be checked.

exercises.prompt: What does the report say about the cost?
options: It was asked about, but no specific amount was given
The report says every proposal is free
exercises.explain: 費用についても質問が出たが、具体的な金額は示されなかった. None of the proposals has an approved cost here.

exercises.prompt: How will people who could not attend be included?
options: They have already voted for the final plan
They can no longer give any view
They will receive the report and can submit views
exercises.explain: The final paragraph plans delivery of the report and receiving their opinions; no completed vote is stated.

exercises.meaning: Constrained continuing debate: discussion over the former site is still continuing.
exercises.explain: The noun modifier をめぐる attaches to 議論; まだ続いている does not say a plan has been approved.

grammar.title: Keep both sides of a comparison
grammar.formation: Verb / i-adjective plain attributive form + 一方（で）; na-adjective + な / である一方（で）; noun + の / である一方（で）. 一方で can also introduce a new sentence.
grammar.explanation: 一方で places another aspect or side beside the first. It can compare two people’s approaches or two effects of one approach. The second clause does not erase the first. A contrast may have favourable and unfavourable sides, but this is not a compulsory positive-negative formula. Here a pause helps questions while interrupting the film’s flow.
grammar.example: 質問しやすい一方で、話の流れが途切れる。
grammar.translation: It’s easier to ask questions, while the flow of the story is interrupted.

examples.ja: {質問|しつもん}しやすい{一方|いっぽう}で、{話|はなし}の{流|なが}れが{途切|とぎ}れる。
examples.en: It’s easier to ask questions, while the flow of the story is interrupted.

examples.ja: ユイは{途中|とちゅう}で{止|と}めたい。{一方|いっぽう}で、{森|もり}さんは{全編|ぜんぺん}を{先|さき}に{見|み}たい。
examples.en: Yui wants to pause partway through. Mori, on the other hand, wants to watch the whole film first.

examples.ja: {説明|せつめい}は{明瞭|めいりょう}な{一方|いっぽう}で、{少|すこ}し{長|なが}い。
examples.en: The explanation is clear, but it’s a little long.

grammar.mistake: Do not choose 一方で or 反面 as uniquely correct solely because one clause is negative. Read both clauses and the stated comparison.

grammar.title: Notice another side of the same approach
grammar.formation: Verb / i-adjective attributive form + 反面; na-adjective + な / である反面; noun + である反面. その反面 can start a contrasting clause.
grammar.explanation: 反面 presents another, contrasting side. In this essay the same pause creates room for a question but may break immersion. It often discusses a benefit and a drawback; it does not require that order in every use. Its scope can overlap with 一方で, so tasks identify the actual effects rather than testing an invented universal dividing line.
grammar.example: 区切りで止めると質問しやすい反面、映画に没頭しにくくなる。
grammar.translation: Pausing at a break makes it easier to ask questions, but it can make it harder to get absorbed in the film.

examples.ja: {区切|くぎ}りで{止|と}めると{質問|しつもん}しやすい{反面|はんめん}、{映画|えいが}に{没頭|ぼっとう}しにくくなる。
examples.en: Pausing at a break makes it easier to ask questions, but it can make it harder to get absorbed in the film.

examples.ja: {全編|ぜんぺん}を{先|さき}に{見|み}ると{流|なが}れがつかめる。その{反面|はんめん}、{途中|とちゅう}の{疑問|ぎもん}を{忘|わす}れることもある。
examples.en: Watching the whole film first lets you follow its flow. On the other hand, you may forget a question you had partway through.

examples.ja: この{方法|ほうほう}は{有効|ゆうこう}な{反面|はんめん}、{時間|じかん}がかかる。
examples.en: This method is effective, but it takes time.

grammar.mistake: Attach な to an ordinary na-adjective here: 有効な反面. Both effects belong to the stated method; do not assign one to a different author.

grammar.title: Read the preferred alternative
grammar.formation: むしろ + clause; X より（も）むしろ Y.
grammar.explanation: むしろ marks an alternative judged more appropriate than the first idea, or corrects a characterisation. Here Mori favours watching the whole film first, rather than pausing at each chapter. The word alone does not show why; read the following reason. It is not a simple replacement for a contrast word meaning “however.”
grammar.example: 途中で何度も止めるより、むしろ最後まで見たい。
grammar.translation: Rather than pause repeatedly, I’d prefer to watch to the end.

examples.ja: {途中|とちゅう}で{何度|なんど}も{止|と}めるより、むしろ{最後|さいご}まで{見|み}たい。
examples.en: Rather than pause repeatedly, I’d prefer to watch to the end.

examples.ja: {質問|しつもん}を{減|へ}らしたいのではない。むしろ、{見|み}た{後|あと}で{話|はなし}を{掘|ほ}り{下|さ}げたい。
examples.en: I don’t want fewer questions. Rather, I want to explore them more deeply after watching.

examples.ja: これは{失敗|しっぱい}ではなく、むしろ{次|つぎ}の{工夫|くふう}につながる{経験|けいけん}だ。
examples.en: This isn’t a failure; it’s more an experience that can lead to improvements next time.

grammar.mistake: Do not infer that Mori opposes questions: the preferred order is film first, discussion afterwards.

grammar.title: Name the aspect on which the views agree
grammar.formation: Attributive clause + 点で; na-adjective + な点で; noun + の点で. A quoted description or noun phrase can be followed by という点で.
grammar.explanation: 点 names an aspect. 質問を大切にするという点で limits the agreement to valuing questions. The two authors still disagree about timing. Compare the same aspect on both sides; similarity on one point does not imply an identical proposal. という点で is useful when stating exactly what the shared point is.
grammar.example: 質問を大切にするという点で、二人の意見は同じだ。
grammar.translation: The two views agree in valuing questions.

examples.ja: {質問|しつもん}を{大切|たいせつ}にするという{点|てん}で、{二人|ふたり}の{意見|いけん}は{同|おな}じだ。
examples.en: The two views agree in valuing questions.

examples.ja: {止|と}める{時点|じてん}という{点|てん}で、{二|ふた}つの{案|あん}は{違|ちが}う。
examples.en: The two proposals differ in when to pause.

examples.ja: {説明|せつめい}が{明瞭|めいりょう}な{点|てん}で、この{案内|あんない}は{読|よ}みやすい。
examples.en: These instructions are easy to read because the explanation is clear.

grammar.mistake: Keep the named aspect attached. Agreement about questions does not mean both authors want to stop during the film.

grammar: two aspects: 一方で / 反面
watch.prompt: Optionally read two reviews or opinions about one film you know. Name one shared purpose, one real difference and one stated limitation in each. Keep the authors distinct; agreement on one aspect is not agreement on every detail.

recycling.reason: The same twelve-minute documentary naturally retrieves 上映 and the recorded owner’s voice from unit 12. The supplementary comparison vocabulary is not forced into spoken lines; a four-percent recent-reference target preserves a realistic planning exchange.

exercises.prompt: Where does Yui initially propose pausing?
options: At the end of the bakery section
In the middle of the owner’s voice
Before showing any of the film
exercises.explain: Yui names the end of the bakery part and explicitly says she does not want to interrupt someone speaking.

exercises.prompt: Why would Yui take questions there?
options: She wants to prevent all conversation after the film
People can ask while they still remember the part
She wants Ren to identify every photograph alone
exercises.explain: 覚えてるうちに聞いてほしくて gives her reason: asking while the memory is fresh.

exercises.prompt: What alternative does Ren suggest?
options: Stop the film after every sentence
Pause just once, not at every break
exercises.explain: Ren suggests 全部の区切りじゃなくて、一回だけ. They will read Mori’s proposal before deciding.

exercises.line: {質問|しつもん}しやすい{一方|いっぽう}で、{話|はなし}の{流|なが}れが{途切|とぎ}れる。
exercises.prompt: Which two effects are held together?
options: Questions are easier, but the flow is interrupted
Questions are impossible, so the film is uninterrupted
Both authors have already approved one final schedule
exercises.explain: Both clauses remain true: easier questioning and interrupted flow. 一方で does not cancel the first clause.

exercises.context: Attach the taught 反面 directly to the na-adjective 有効: effective, but time-consuming.
exercises.line: この{方法|ほうほう}は{有効|ゆうこう}＿＿{反面|はんめん}、{時間|じかん}がかかる。
exercises.explain: A na-adjective takes な before 反面 here. である is another valid attachment but is not offered as a wrong answer.

exercises.line: {質問|しつもん}しやすい{反面|はんめん}、{映画|えいが}に{没頭|ぼっとう}しにくい。
exercises.prompt: What drawback does this sentence state?
options: The owner’s voice has been deleted
It is impossible for anyone to ask a question
It is harder to get absorbed in the film
exercises.explain: 没頭しにくい names a difficulty getting absorbed. The sentence still says questions are easier.

exercises.prompt: What is Yui’s main proposal?
options: Pause at section breaks to take questions
Show the whole film first, then replay selected parts
Ask for long written responses before the film
exercises.explain: The opening proposes breaks for questions. A single pause is later offered as an option for many first-time viewers, not a decided replacement.

exercises.prompt: What does Yui explicitly avoid interrupting?
options: The owner’s voice while it is playing
The preparation of paper and pens
exercises.explain: 店主の声が流れている途中では止めない is an explicit limitation on her proposal.

exercises.prompt: What would Yui do if the questions run long?
options: Require only the archive staff to speak
Take the remaining questions after the screening
exercises.explain: 質問が長くなったら、残りは上映の後に聞く. The proposal preserves later questions.

exercises.meaning: Constrained two-effect statement: questions are easier, while the flow is interrupted.
exercises.explain: The tiles preserve both effects of the same approach; this is not a free-expression fluency score.

exercises.prompt: What order does Mori propose?
options: Watch the whole film, then talk
Discuss every photograph before the film starts
exercises.explain: Mori says 最後まで見てから話したい. The film is twelve minutes long.

exercises.prompt: How would Mori help people remember questions?
options: Tell them that questions are forbidden
Give them paper for short notes
Make Yui read every question during the film
exercises.explain: Mori suggests メモ用の紙. Yui will prepare paper and pens.

exercises.prompt: What does Mori say about replaying the bakery owner’s voice?
options: They will remove it before the event
They can return to that part after watching the whole film
exercises.explain: Mori agrees to go back to that part and invite memories. Mori’s preference is an order, not a ban on revisiting material.

exercises.line: {途中|とちゅう}で{止|と}めるより、むしろ{全編|ぜんぺん}を{先|さき}に{見|み}たい。
exercises.prompt: Which alternative does むしろ mark as preferred?
options: Do not watch the film at all
exercises.explain: The preferred alternative follows むしろ. The sentence does not by itself abolish discussion afterwards.

exercises.line: {質問|しつもん}を{大切|たいせつ}にするという{点|てん}で、{二人|ふたり}は{同|おな}じだ。
exercises.prompt: How far does the stated agreement extend?
options: Every detail of their proposals is identical
They both value questions; the timing may still differ
Both reject all questions during and after the film
exercises.explain: という点で identifies the shared aspect. It does not make their schedules identical.

exercises.prompt: Read both opinions. What do both authors want the event to provide?
options: Silent viewing with no discussion afterwards
A long written response from every viewer
A chance for people to ask questions and share memories
exercises.explain: A wants questions and shared memories at breaks and afterwards. B wants questions and discussion after the whole film. Their shared purpose is conversation.

exercises.prompt: Read both opinions. What is the central difference between the proposals?
options: Whether to pause at section breaks or show the whole film first
Whether the film concerns the shopping street or a railway
Whether the film is twelve minutes or two hours long
exercises.explain: Both discuss the same twelve-minute film. A favours section-break questions; B favours the whole film first, then discussion and selective replay.

exercises.prompt: Read both opinions. Which concern is assigned to the correct author?
options: A says nobody remembers questions; B says everyone must write an essay
A worries pauses interrupt immersion; B worries lengthy note-taking distracts from the images
A worries about a railway closure; B worries about the film’s ticket price
exercises.explain: A acknowledges flow and immersion may suffer. B explicitly notes that focusing too much on writing can make someone miss the images. Neither concern means the whole proposal is rejected.

exercises.prompt: Read both opinions. Which description of later questions is supported?
options: Only A allows any later questions; B forbids them
Both require every question to be asked before viewing
Both allow questions afterwards; B also proposes replaying needed parts
exercises.explain: A moves remaining questions after the screening if they take too long. B puts discussion afterwards and offers replay of selected parts.

tiles: {質問|しつもん}を{大切|たいせつ}にする
{二人|ふたり}の{意見|いけん}は
exercises.meaning: Constrained shared aspect: the two views agree in valuing questions.
exercises.explain: The sentence confines the agreement to a named aspect; it does not declare the proposals identical.

lessons.title: A bag of cakes, without losing one
lessons.description: Tamura and Mori chat at a bakery before a community screening.
lessons.canDo: Recognise regional copulas, negatives and everyday words while following a practical plan

lessons.title: The teacher is coming for tea
lessons.description: Two colleagues set out cups and keep the bag away from steam.
lessons.canDo: Track respectful regional references to a teacher and distinguish a question from a later outcome

grammar.title: Hear the regional copula in an ordinary chat
grammar.formation: Noun / na-adjective stem + や; past やった; explanatory noun + なんや, verb clause + んや. Do not attach copula や directly to a plain verb or i-adjective.
grammar.explanation: Tamura uses や where the corresponding standard casual copula is だ. そや is agreement, and ほんまや responds to something just noticed. Here the words belong to friendly off-duty conversation. A speaker can also use standard polite language in a business call. Learn the sentence meaning first, without assuming every Kansai speaker chooses identical endings.
grammar.example: ここ、行きつけの店や。
grammar.translation: This is a shop I often go to.

examples.ja: ここ、{行|い}きつけの{店|みせ}や。
examples.en: This is a shop I often go to.

examples.ja: あの{湯飲|ゆの}み、{先生|せんせい}のお{気|き}に{入|い}りやったな。
examples.en: That cup was the teacher’s favourite, wasn’t it?

examples.ja: ほんまや。{紙袋|かみぶくろ}が{濡|ぬ}れてる。
examples.en: You’re right. The paper bag’s wet.

grammar.mistake: Recognise や as a copula here, not the standard list particle in パンやお茶. ほんまや is not a rule that i-adjectives take や.

grammar.title: Recognise the negative before judging the plan
grammar.formation: Selected forms here: 食べる → 食べへん; 分かる → 分からへん; 足りる → 足りへん; 濡れる → 濡れへん. Regional and individual alternatives exist.
grammar.explanation: へん makes the selected verbs negative: 食べへん is not eat, not an extra positive action. Tamura declines a taste so eight purchased cakes remain eight. Recognise the whole form in its situation. Godan stems and short verbs have regional variants; some surface forms can overlap potential forms. This lesson does not ask you to derive every verb with one universal stem rule.
grammar.example: 今は食べへん。会場で食べる。
grammar.translation: I won’t eat one now. I’ll have it at the venue.

examples.ja: {今|いま}は{食|た}べへん。{会場|かいじょう}で{食|た}べる。
examples.en: I won’t eat one now. I’ll have it at the venue.

examples.ja: これだけやと、{人数|にんずう}が{分|わ}からへん。
examples.en: From this alone, I can’t tell how many people there are.

examples.ja: {棚|たな}の{上|うえ}なら{紙袋|かみぶくろ}は{濡|ぬ}れへん。
examples.en: On top of the shelf, the paper bag won’t get wet.

grammar.mistake: Do not translate every regional e-stem + へん as can’t: form and meaning vary by area and context. Here eight minus one would not be enough, so 足りへん refers to a shortage.

grammar.title: Follow everyday regional words through the situation
grammar.formation: めっちゃ + description; ほんま / ほんまに; なんぼ in a price question; おおきに for thanks; ほな as then; あかん with the surrounding action.
grammar.explanation: めっちゃ intensifies a description; ほんま responds to truth or surprise; なんぼ asks a price here. おおきに thanks Mori for carrying a bag, not a greeting. ほな moves to the next step. In ここに置いたらあかん？, Tamura asks whether putting the bag there is a bad idea. Context supplies the force. These words do not by themselves identify a stranger’s origin or make a sentence formally polite.
grammar.example: これ、なんぼ？二百円？めっちゃ安いな。
grammar.translation: How much is this? Two hundred yen? That’s really cheap.

examples.ja: これ、なんぼ？{二百円|にひゃくえん}？めっちゃ{安|やす}いな。
examples.en: How much is this? Two hundred yen? That’s really cheap.

examples.ja: {紙袋|かみぶくろ}、{持|も}ってくれておおきに。
examples.en: Thanks for carrying the paper bag.

examples.ja: ここに{置|お}いたらあかん？ほな、{棚|たな}に{置|お}くわ。
examples.en: Shouldn’t I put it here? Then I’ll put it on the shelf.

grammar.mistake: あかん can judge something as no good or disallow an action; use the actual sentence. めっちゃ is casual emphasis, not a dependable geographical label.

grammar.title: Follow whose action receives regional respect
grammar.formation: Selected recognition forms: 来る → きはる; 使う → 使いはる; 待っている → 待ってはる. Godan attachment and ongoing forms differ across regions.
grammar.explanation: Tamura refers to Satō-sensei’s arrival, cup choice and waiting with はる. Respect concerns the person doing the action, not simply who hears the sentence. The tone can remain friendly. Regional use is broader than standard formal honorifics and varies with relationships; this is not a universal substitute for workplace keigo. Focus on the doer and the action in these lines, with 来る written きはる to make the reading explicit.
grammar.example: 先生は三時半にきはる。
grammar.translation: The teacher is coming at half past three.

examples.ja: {先生|せんせい}は{三時半|さんじはん}にきはる。
examples.en: The teacher is coming at half past three.

examples.ja: {先生|せんせい}、この{湯飲|ゆの}みを{使|つか}いはるかな。
examples.en: I wonder whether the teacher will use this cup.

examples.ja: {先生|せんせい}が{店先|みせさき}で{待|ま}ってはる。
examples.en: The teacher’s waiting outside the shop.

grammar.mistake: The teacher performs these actions. Do not choose Mori merely because Mori hears the line, or derive all regional はる forms from the standard masu stem.

readings.title: Mori’s diary after the tea break
paragraphs: {土曜日|どようび}の{午後|ごご}、{田村|たむら}さんとお{茶|ちゃ}の{準備|じゅんび}をした。{先生|せんせい}が{何時|なんじ}に{来|く}るか{聞|き}くと、「{三時半|さんじはん}にきはるって」と{教|おし}えてくれた。{朝|あさ}に{買|か}ったケーキは{八個|はっこ}。{私|わたし}が{一個|いっこ}{味見|あじみ}しようと{言|い}ったら、「{今|いま}は{食|た}べへん」と{断|ことわ}られた。{残|のこ}りが{七個|ななこ}になるからだった。

{田村|たむら}さんは{小|ちい}さい{湯飲|ゆの}みを{出|だ}して、「{先生|せんせい}、{今日|きょう}はこれ{使|つか}いはるかな」と{言|い}った。{前|まえ}のお{気|き}に{入|い}りは{一|ひと}つ{割|わ}れてしまった。{田村|たむら}さんが{新|あたら}しい{湯飲|ゆの}みを{台|だい}の{真|ま}ん{中|なか}に{置|お}こうとしたので、つい「{割|わ}ったのは{僕|ぼく}じゃないよ」と{答|こた}えた。{田村|たむら}さんは{笑|わら}っていた。

{先生|せんせい}は{約束|やくそく}の{時間|じかん}に{到着|とうちゃく}した。{店先|みせさき}に{立|た}っていたので、{田村|たむら}さんが「{先生|せんせい}、{外|そと}で{待|ま}ってはる」と{知|し}らせてくれた。{私|わたし}が{中|なか}に{案内|あんない}すると、{先生|せんせい}は{棚|たな}の{上|うえ}の{紙袋|かみぶくろ}を{見|み}て、「いいにおいがするね」と{言|い}った。

{四時|よじ}から{映画|えいが}を{見|み}て、その{後|あと}で{急須|きゅうす}にお{湯|ゆ}を{入|い}れた。{先生|せんせい}は{小|ちい}さい{湯飲|ゆの}みを{使|つか}い、{昔|むかし}のパン{屋|や}の{話|はなし}をしてくれた。ケーキは{八個|はっこ}ともなくなった。{田村|たむら}さんが「ほんま、{朝|あさ}に{買|か}ってよかったな」と{言|い}ったので、{私|わたし}も{同|おな}じ{気持|きも}ちだと{答|こた}えた。

watch.prompt: Optionally find a short conversation in media you already use. With its transcript, locate one regional negative and one はる reference; identify the action and doer. Listen to the original speaker for accent and timing. A transcript can support form recognition without proving you can produce the regional accent.

recycling.reason: The screening from units 12–13 motivates buying eight sweets and keeping rustling bags closed during the film. Recent references are counted only where actually spoken. Extra headwords and linguistic terms remain supplementary rather than distorting this friendly conversation.

exercises.prompt: Why does Tamura know this shop?
options: It is a shop Tamura often visits
exercises.explain: 行きつけの店 means a shop one regularly visits; ownership is not stated.

exercises.prompt: What price does Mori give for one cake?
exercises.explain: 一個二百円 is the unit price; eight is the chosen quantity.

exercises.prompt: Why does Tamura refuse to taste one now?
options: It would leave only seven of the eight they need
exercises.explain: Tamura says 足りへん: eight minus one would leave them short. There is no dislike or shop rule.
店や is the copula after the noun, corresponding to standard casual 店だ.
exercises.line: ここ、{行|い}きつけの{店|みせ}＿＿。
exercises.context: Recover Tamura’s regional copula after a noun: ここ、行きつけの店＿＿。

exercises.prompt: Read 今は食べへん。会場で食べる。 Which meaning fits?
options: I have already eaten at the venue
I won’t eat now; I’ll eat at the venue
I won’t eat at the venue either
exercises.explain: へん negates the first action only. The second sentence says the later eating will happen.
exercises.line: {今|いま}は{食|た}べへん。{会場|かいじょう}で{食|た}べる。

exercises.prompt: Mori offers to carry the bag. What does Tamura’s おおきに do here?
options: Ask how much the bag costs
exercises.explain: It responds to the offer with thanks. The preceding action identifies its function.
exercises.line: おおきに。

exercises.meaning: Constrained recall: this cake smells really fragrant.
exercises.explain: めっちゃ intensifies 香ばしい. The tiles practise this supplied sentence, not free dialect production.

exercises.prompt: Why is Tamura glad they stopped by in the morning?
options: The cakes can sell out by midday
The screening begins in the morning
exercises.explain: The message says 昼には売り切れになることもある. The film starts at four.

exercises.prompt: Why will they wait until after the film to open the bag?
options: The bag belongs to the teacher
Rustling could make the recorded voice hard to hear
The cakes must be baked again
exercises.explain: がさがさ音がして声が聞こえへん is a listening problem caused by the rustling bag.

exercises.prompt: What would make them skip the stop to look at the shop photo?
options: The teacher uses a smaller cup
exercises.explain: If the train time is near, they will go directly to the station. The detour is conditional, not cancelled already.

exercises.prompt: What arrival time does Tamura report for the teacher?
exercises.explain: 三時半にきはる gives the teacher’s arrival. It is not the four-o’clock film start.

exercises.prompt: What does Mori say about the old cup?
options: It is too expensive to use
One broke; a smaller one is available
The teacher has taken every cup home
exercises.explain: 一つ割れちゃって reports the break. 小さいのならある offers the available alternative.

exercises.prompt: Why does Mori suggest putting the bag on the shelf?
options: The shelf is where the teacher always sits
Steam would make it wet in the first spot
exercises.explain: Mori names the steam risk and then suggests the shelf; Tamura accepts the dry alternative.

exercises.prompt: Whose waiting receives the respectful はる form in this sentence?
exercises.explain: 先生が names the doer. This is an explicit subject question, not guessing a person from an accent.
exercises.line: {先生|せんせい}が{店先|みせさき}で{待|ま}ってはる。

exercises.prompt: What does this line report?
options: The teacher is coming at half past three
exercises.explain: きはる is the selected respectful regional form of 来る; the teacher is the subject.
exercises.line: {先生|せんせい}は{三時半|さんじはん}にきはる。

exercises.meaning: Constrained recognition/recall: I wonder if the teacher will use this cup.
exercises.explain: The teacher is the doer and かな leaves the choice uncertain; it does not say the cup has been chosen already.

exercises.prompt: Who suggested tasting a cake, and who declined?
options: The teacher suggested it; both declined
exercises.explain: The diary’s 私 is Mori. Tamura responds 今は食べへん. Keep narrator and quoted speaker separate.

exercises.prompt: What did Mori do after Tamura noticed the teacher outside?
options: Sent the teacher to the station
Started the film without the teacher
exercises.explain: Tamura reports the waiting; Mori then guides the teacher in. Mori is not the waiting teacher.

exercises.prompt: What happened to the smaller cup by the end of the diary?
exercises.explain: The earlier dialogue asks 使いはるかな, an open possibility; the later diary reports actual use.

exercises.prompt: How many cakes remained after the tea break?
options: Seven, because Tamura ate one early
exercises.explain: 八個ともなくなった means all eight were gone. Tamura had declined the early taste.
