lessons.title: A chorus worth waking up for
lessons.description: Kenta and Misaki react to a concert clip and plan an extra ticket sale.
lessons.canDo: Interpret enthusiastic and worried slang reactions while following a real plan

lessons.title: One extra zero in the message
lessons.description: Two friends laugh at a typing error and keep tomorrow’s purchase uncertain.
lessons.canDo: Read laughter cues, uncertainty and a later confirmation in peer messages

grammar.title: Hear genuine enthusiasm and serious intent
grammar.formation: ガチで + action or evaluation; ガチ？ as a casual reaction. Not the tendency suffix 〜がち.
grammar.explanation: In this peer conversation, ガチで marks genuine effort or an emphatic reaction. Kenta is serious about getting tickets and really impressed by the singing. It does not turn an opinion into verified evidence. Use the action and surrounding reply to understand it. Usage checked 6 October 2026 against dated publisher and teacher examples; this is recognition, not a claim that everyone uses the same slang.
grammar.example: ガチで行きたい。
grammar.translation: I really want to go.

examples.ja: ガチで{行|い}きたい。
examples.en: I really want to go.

examples.ja: あの{歌声|うたごえ}、ガチで{好|す}き。
examples.en: I really love that singing voice.

examples.ja: ガチで{練習|れんしゅう}したの？
examples.en: Did you seriously practise for it?

grammar.mistake: Do not confuse ガチで with 遅れがち, which describes a tendency. A concert opinion is still an opinion.

grammar.title: Use the situation to interpret やばい
grammar.formation: やばい as an i-adjective; やばかった for past; やばすぎ for strong casual emphasis.
grammar.explanation: やばい can react to trouble or to something strikingly good. Kenta likes the song but worries about tickets being sold out. The surrounding facts and response determine the meaning; the word alone cannot choose between them. Positive uses are documented in older teacher lessons as well as negative ones. Recognition notes checked 6 October 2026; no single age group or fixed emotional pitch is assigned.
grammar.example: この歌声、やばい。もう一回聞きたい。
grammar.translation: That singing voice is amazing. I want to hear it again.

examples.ja: この{歌声|うたごえ}、やばい。もう{一回|いっかい}{聞|き}きたい。
examples.en: That singing voice is amazing. I want to hear it again.

examples.ja: やばい、{終電|しゅうでん}に{間|ま}に{合|あ}わない。
examples.en: Oh no, I’m going to miss the last train.

examples.ja: やばかった。でも{電車|でんしゃ}には{乗|の}れた。
examples.en: That was close. But I caught the train.

grammar.mistake: Choose admiration or trouble from the actual situation. Do not translate every やばい as dangerous, or every やばい as amazing.

grammar.title: Recognise clipped すぎ without losing the base form
grammar.formation: Verb masu stem / i-adjective without final い / na-adjective stem + すぎる; casual standalone すぎ. いい → よすぎ.
grammar.explanation: This retrieves earlier すぎる and adds recognition of clipped reactions. 高すぎ can complain about a price, while 歌声よすぎ praises a singer. The same form need not be negative. Keep the correct stem: 早い becomes 早すぎ, いい becomes よすぎ and 寝る becomes 寝すぎる. The lesson practises these selected attachments, not every playful noun formation found online.
grammar.example: 字、小さすぎ。読めない。
grammar.translation: The text’s too small. I can’t read it.

examples.ja: {字|じ}、{小|ちい}さすぎ。{読|よ}めない。
examples.en: The text’s too small. I can’t read it.

examples.ja: この{歌声|うたごえ}、よすぎ。
examples.en: That singing voice is so good.

examples.ja: {寝|ね}すぎた。もう{十時|じゅうじ}だ。
examples.en: I slept too long. It’s already ten.

grammar.mistake: Drop い from ordinary i-adjectives; use よ, not い, for いい. Positive enthusiasm and a practical complaint can both use すぎ.

grammar.title: Leave a possible outcome uncertain
grammar.formation: ワンチャン + possible outcome; often followed by かも / かもしれない. Not a promise or a fixed probability.
grammar.explanation: ワンチャン frames a possibility in this casual plan. Extra tickets might be sold tomorrow, but Kenta and Misaki have not bought them. A later message can confirm what actually happened. It does not always mean exactly one chance, nor does it supply a numerical probability. Dated 2020/2025 authored sources and usage checked 6 October 2026; official notices state concrete times instead.
grammar.example: ワンチャン、追加のチケット買えるかも。
grammar.translation: We might be able to get the extra tickets.

examples.ja: ワンチャン、{追加|ついか}のチケット{買|か}えるかも。
examples.en: We might be able to get the extra tickets.

examples.ja: {今|いま}{出|で}れば、ワンチャン{間|ま}に{合|あ}う。
examples.en: If we leave now, we might make it.

examples.ja: ワンチャンあると{思|おも}って、{確認|かくにん}した。
examples.en: I checked because I thought there might be a chance.

grammar.mistake: Possible purchase is not a completed purchase. Read かも, dates and later confirmations before deciding what is certain.

grammar.title: Read a laughter reaction in a typed exchange
grammar.formation: 草 / 笑 / w as laughter cues in selected messages; 草 is read くさ. Literal 草 still means grass in other contexts.
grammar.explanation: In Misaki’s message, 草 responds to Kenta’s impossible 100 o’clock typo with laughter. The reply and their friendly joking support that interpretation. Different people can hear laughter, teasing or sarcasm differently, so inspect the exchange rather than assuming every 草 is ridicule. This is a new contextual sense of the already-taught spelling 草, not a second grass vocabulary test. Usage checked 6 October 2026; dictionary editors’ dated interviews support the sense and variation.
grammar.example: 「百時集合」って書いてて草。
grammar.translation: You wrote “meet at 100 o’clock,” lol.

examples.ja: 「{百時|ひゃくじ}{集合|しゅうごう}」って{書|か}いてて{草|くさ}。
examples.en: You wrote “meet at 100 o’clock,” lol.

examples.ja: {笑|わら}った。{同|おな}じ{打|う}ち{間違|まちが}い、{私|わたし}もした。
examples.en: That made me laugh. I made the same typo.

examples.ja: {庭|にわ}の{草|くさ}を{抜|ぬ}いた。
examples.en: I pulled the weeds in the garden.

grammar.mistake: 草 does not mean laughter in every sentence; the garden example is literal vegetation. Friendly laughter is not automatically ridicule.

dialogues.title: Tomorrow at ten, not tonight

lines.speaker: Kenta
lines.line: このライブの{動画|どうが}、{見|み}た？サビ、やばすぎ。
lines.romaji: Kono raibu no dōga, mita? Sabi, yabasugi.
lines.meaning: Have you seen this concert clip? The chorus is amazing.

lines.speaker: Misaki
lines.line: {見|み}た。{映像|えいぞう}もきれい。{歌声|うたごえ}よすぎ。{最後|さいご}、{何回|なんかい}も{戻|もど}しちゃった。
lines.romaji: Mita. Eizō mo kirei. Utagoe yosugi. Saigo, nankai mo modoshichatta.
lines.meaning: Yeah. The video looks beautiful too. The singing is so good. I kept replaying the end.

lines.speaker: Kenta
lines.line: ガチで{行|い}きたい。チケット、まだある？
lines.romaji: Gachi de ikitai. Chiketto, mada aru?
lines.meaning: I really want to go. Are there any tickets left?

lines.speaker: Misaki
lines.line: {今|いま}の{分|ぶん}は{完売|かんばい}だって。
lines.romaji: Ima no bun wa kanbai datte.
lines.meaning: It says the current batch is sold out.

lines.speaker: Kenta
lines.line: やばい、{遅|おそ}すぎた。
lines.romaji: Yabai, ososugita.
lines.meaning: Oh no, I left it too late.

lines.speaker: Misaki
lines.line: でも{追加|ついか}の{販売|はんばい}があるよ。{明日|あした}の{十時|じゅうじ}から。
lines.romaji: Demo tsuika no hanbai ga aru yo. Ashita no jūji kara.
lines.meaning: But there’s another batch going on sale. From ten tomorrow.

lines.speaker: Kenta
lines.line: ワンチャン{買|か}える？
lines.romaji: Wanchan kaeru?
lines.meaning: So we might get some?

lines.speaker: Misaki
lines.line: うん、ワンチャンね。{先着|せんちゃく}だから、{九時五十分|くじごじゅっぷん}にはページ{開|ひら}いとこ。
lines.romaji: Un, wanchan ne. Senchaku dakara, kuji gojuppun ni wa pēji hiraitoko.
lines.meaning: Yeah, maybe. It’s first come, first served, so let’s have the page open by nine fifty.

lines.speaker: Kenta
lines.line: {朝|あさ}？{早|はや}すぎ。{休|やす}みの{日|ひ}なのに。
lines.romaji: Asa? Hayasugi. Yasumi no hi na noni.
lines.meaning: In the morning? That’s so early for a day off.

lines.speaker: Misaki
lines.line: {十時|じゅうじ}だよ。ガチで{行|い}きたいんでしょ？
lines.romaji: Jūji da yo. Gachi de ikitai n desho?
lines.meaning: It’s ten. You really want to go, don’t you?

lines.speaker: Kenta
lines.line: {行|い}きたい。ガチで{起|お}きる。{目覚|めざ}まし{二|ふた}つにする。
lines.romaji: Ikitai. Gachi de okiru. Mezamashi futatsu ni suru.
lines.meaning: I do. I’ll definitely get up. I’ll set two alarms.

lines.speaker: Misaki
lines.line: {二|ふた}つとも{止|と}めて{寝|ね}すぎないでよ。
lines.romaji: Futatsu tomo tomete nesuginai de yo.
lines.meaning: Don’t turn both off and oversleep.

lines.speaker: Kenta
lines.line: そこまで{信用|しんよう}ない？{買|か}えたら、{一緒|いっしょ}に{行|い}こう。
lines.romaji: Soko made shinyō nai? Kaetara, issho ni ikō.
lines.meaning: Do you trust me that little? If I get tickets, let’s go together.

lines.speaker: Misaki
lines.line: もちろん。あのサビ、{生|なま}で{聞|き}けたらやばいね。
lines.romaji: Mochiron. Ano sabi, nama de kiketara yabai ne.
lines.meaning: Of course. Hearing that chorus live would be amazing.

dialogues.scene: Kenta and Misaki watch a concert clip and prepare for tomorrow morning’s first-come ticket sale. The concert is next month.

dialogues.title: Meet at 100 o’clock?

lines.speaker: Misaki
lines.line: さっきのメッセージ、「{百時|ひゃくじ}{集合|しゅうごう}」ってなってたよ。
lines.romaji: Sakki no messēji, hyakuji shūgō tte natteta yo.
lines.meaning: Your message just said “meet at 100 o’clock.”

lines.speaker: Kenta
lines.line: ガチ？{十時|じゅうじ}って{打|う}ったつもりだった。
lines.romaji: Gachi? Jūji tte utta tsumori datta.
lines.meaning: Seriously? I meant to type ten.

lines.speaker: Misaki
lines.line: ガチ。「{遠|とお}すぎて{草|くさ}」って{返|かえ}した。
lines.romaji: Gachi. Tōsugite kusa tte kaeshita.
lines.meaning: Seriously. I replied, “That’s so far off, lol.”

lines.speaker: Kenta
lines.line: {百時|ひゃくじ}まで{待|ま}つの？それは{長|なが}すぎ。
lines.romaji: Hyakuji made matsu no? Sore wa nagasugi.
lines.meaning: Wait until 100 o’clock? That’s far too long.

lines.speaker: Misaki
lines.line: だから{笑|わら}ったんだって。{私|わたし}も、ゼロ{増|ふ}やしたことある。
lines.romaji: Dakara waratta n datte. Watashi mo, zero fuyashita koto aru.
lines.meaning: That’s why I laughed! I’ve added an extra zero before too.

lines.speaker: Kenta
lines.line: {通知|つうち}が{多|おお}すぎて、{見落|みお}としてた。{今|いま}{直|なお}す。
lines.romaji: Tsūchi ga ōsugite, miotoshiteta. Ima naosu.
lines.meaning: I had so many notifications I missed it. I’ll fix it now.

lines.speaker: Misaki
lines.line: {直|なお}すのは{時刻|じこく}だけね。{販売|はんばい}は{明日|あした}だよ。
lines.romaji: Naosu no wa jikoku dake ne. Hanbai wa ashita da yo.
lines.meaning: Just fix the time. The sale is tomorrow.

lines.speaker: Kenta
lines.line: {分|わ}かってる。ワンチャン{今|いま}{買|か}えるかと{思|おも}って、{見|み}たけど。
lines.romaji: Wakatteru. Wanchan ima kaeru ka to omotte, mita kedo.
lines.meaning: I know. I did check, though, in case we could buy them now.

lines.speaker: Misaki
lines.line: まだ{受付前|うけつけまえ}。ガチで{寝|ね}る{前|まえ}に{時刻|じこく}を{確認|かくにん}してよ。
lines.romaji: Mada uketsuke mae. Gachi de neru mae ni jikoku o kakunin shite yo.
lines.meaning: Sales haven’t opened yet. Seriously, check the time before you go to sleep.

lines.speaker: Kenta
lines.line: {今夜|こんや}は{動画|どうが}{見|み}すぎない。やばい、もう{十一時|じゅういちじ}じゃん。
lines.romaji: Kon’ya wa dōga misuginai. Yabai, mō jūichiji jan.
lines.meaning: I won’t watch too many videos tonight. Oh no, it’s already eleven.

lines.speaker: Misaki
lines.line: {明日|あした}{買|か}えたら、また「{草|くさ}」って{送|おく}る？
lines.romaji: Ashita kaetara, mata kusa tte okuru?
lines.meaning: If we get tickets tomorrow, shall I send “lol” again?

lines.speaker: Kenta
lines.line: その{時|とき}は「やばい！」でしょ。ガチでうれしいから。
lines.romaji: Sono toki wa yabai desho. Gachi de ureshii kara.
lines.meaning: Then it should be “amazing!” Because I’ll be really happy.

grammar: contextual やばい / ガチで
uncertain ワンチャン versus a confirmed later event
草 / 笑 / w in the surrounding exchange
watch.prompt: Optionally use a short peer conversation or a few comments from media you already read. Identify a positive and a negative reaction from their context, and separate an uncertain plan from a later confirmation. Slang spelling and usage vary by community and period.

recycling.reason: The clip’s beautiful video naturally retrieves 映像. Earlier first-come sales, notifications and uncertainty fit the plan. Recent regional and essay headwords do not belong in this peer chat; the one-percent recent-reference exception prevents vocabulary quotas from distorting the dialogue.

exercises.prompt: Why does Misaki replay the end of the clip?
options: The ticket price is hidden at the end
exercises.explain: 歌声よすぎ is enthusiastic praise; Misaki says the end was replayed repeatedly.

exercises.prompt: What goes wrong before Misaki mentions the extra batch?
options: The current batch of tickets is sold out
Kenta lost a ticket already bought
exercises.explain: 今の分は完売 and 遅すぎた describe missing the current sale; the later extra batch is still possible.

exercises.prompt: When should they have the sales page open?
exercises.explain: The sale starts at ten tomorrow; Misaki proposes opening the page by nine fifty, because it is first come, first served.

exercises.prompt: Which meaning fits Kenta’s comment?
exercises.line: ガチで{行|い}きたい。
options: Kenta has already bought a ticket
exercises.explain: ガチで emphasises serious desire here; it is not 〜がち or a report of a completed purchase.

exercises.prompt: Which reaction fits both lines?
exercises.line: この{歌声|うたごえ}、やばい。もう{一回|いっかい}{聞|き}きたい。
options: A warning about the last train
exercises.explain: Wanting to hear it again supports admiration. やばい alone does not fix the polarity.

exercises.context: Choose the stem from いい to praise this singing as extremely good.
exercises.line: この{歌声|うたごえ}、＿＿すぎ。
exercises.explain: いい uses the よい stem よ before すぎ. This is praise, not necessarily a complaint.

exercises.prompt: How are the extra tickets allocated?
exercises.explain: The message explicitly says 抽選じゃなくて先着順. No purchase is yet confirmed.

exercises.prompt: Who should buy the two tickets?
exercises.explain: Misaki buys 自分の一枚 and asks Kenta for 自分の分. They report if only one succeeds.

exercises.prompt: When is the actual concert?
options: Tomorrow at ten in the morning
exercises.explain: Tomorrow’s ten o’clock is the sale; the performance is next month, with entry at 5:30 and start at six.

exercises.prompt: When do they intend to choose their train time?
options: After they know whether both tickets were bought
exercises.explain: 二枚買えたかどうか分かってから sets the condition; checking the last train is preparation, not a report that they missed it.

exercises.prompt: What does Kenta correct?
exercises.explain: Kenta intended 十時 but sent 百時. Misaki says the date tomorrow should stay.

exercises.prompt: What supports Misaki’s friendly laughter?
options: Misaki says Kenta is not allowed to attend
Misaki announces the event was cancelled
Misaki says the same extra-zero mistake has happened before
exercises.explain: Misaki laughs at the impossible time and shares the same experience. The dialogue supports friendly joking, not exclusion.

exercises.prompt: Has either person bought a ticket during this conversation?
options: No; sales have not opened yet
exercises.explain: まだ受付前 and 明日 make the present purchase unconfirmed. ワンチャン is a possibility.

exercises.prompt: What is certain from this message alone?
exercises.line: ワンチャン、{追加|ついか}のチケット{買|か}えるかも。
options: The tickets have already been bought
The speaker thinks purchase might be possible
The chance is exactly one percent
exercises.explain: ワンチャン with かも leaves it possible. It is neither completed nor a numerical probability.

exercises.prompt: Read the friend’s response to an impossible 100 o’clock typo. What does 草 do here?
exercises.line: 「{百時|ひゃくじ}{集合|しゅうごう}」って{書|か}いてて{草|くさ}。
options: Confirms the tickets have been bought
exercises.explain: The message is reacting to a typo with laughter. Literal garden 草 is a different context; this is not the earlier grass word quiz.

exercises.meaning: Constrained recall: We might be able to get the extra tickets.
exercises.explain: かも preserves uncertainty; this does not say we managed to buy them.

exercises.prompt: Why was Misaki’s message not immediately marked as read?
options: Misaki had not sent a message
The ticket office had closed forever
exercises.explain: The passage states 健太は通知を見落としていた. Delay is not proof of refusal or a broken service.

exercises.prompt: Which response reinforces Misaki’s friendly joking?
options: Giving a new concert cancellation notice
Saying the same typo has happened before and adding a laughing sticker
Demanding that Kenta stop speaking forever
exercises.explain: The shared typo and laughing-face sticker support this exchange’s tone. 草 is not universally harmless or universally ridicule.

exercises.prompt: What changes between Friday night and Saturday morning?
options: A garden has grown at the venue
Possible purchase becomes two confirmed one-ticket purchases
exercises.explain: Friday 買えるかも is uncertain; Saturday each person purchases 一枚ずつ and confirms 買えた.

exercises.prompt: What remains to be decided after both purchases?
options: Whether the sale starts at 100 o’clock
exercises.explain: 電車の時間はこれから決める. Both purchases are explicit and the earlier typo was corrected.

grammar.title: Introduce your own experience respectfully
grammar.formation: 申す → 申します; する → いたします; いる → おります; suitable お/ご + stem + いたします.
grammar.explanation: This capstone retrieves earlier keigo while answering real questions. 申します introduces your name deferentially to the listener; いたします and おります describe your side. A respected interviewer’s action needs a different form. You can describe your experience plainly with polite endings rather than replacing every verb. Special verbs and prefix choices are lexical; the template is not universal.
grammar.example: バオと申します。
grammar.translation: My name is Bao.

examples.ja: バオと{申|もう}します。
examples.en: My name is Bao.

examples.ja: {実習|じっしゅう}では{案内|あんない}の{作成|さくせい}を{担当|たんとう}しておりました。
examples.en: During the internship, I worked on making the brochure.

examples.ja: {経験|けいけん}についてご{説明|せつめい}いたします。
examples.en: I’ll explain my experience.

grammar.mistake: Do not honour your own action with おっしゃいます or ご覧になります. More elaborate keigo is not required in every answer.

grammar.title: Change company references with the medium
grammar.formation: 御社 (おんしゃ): spoken reference to the addressee’s company; 貴社 (きしゃ): written reference; 弊社 (へいしゃ): one’s own company, externally.
grammar.explanation: The applicant says 御社 during this interview and writes 貴社 in an application. Ishikawa can use 弊社 for the company he represents. This is business-language retrieval, not a new official N2 rule. Identify whose company is meant before translating the form. The learner has completed an internship but has not yet received a job offer.
grammar.example: 御社の仕事に関心があります。
grammar.translation: I’m interested in your company’s work.

examples.ja: {御社|おんしゃ}の{仕事|しごと}に{関心|かんしん}があります。
examples.en: I’m interested in your company’s work.

examples.ja: {貴社|きしゃ}への{志望動機|しぼうどうき}を{書|か}きました。
examples.en: I wrote my reason for applying to your company.

examples.ja: {弊社|へいしゃ}では{入社|にゅうしゃ}{後|ご}に{研修|けんしゅう}を{行|おこな}います。
examples.en: At our company, training takes place after joining.

grammar.mistake: Do not translate every 社 expression as my company. Spoken and written references should fit their medium.

grammar.title: Ask the interviewer without reversing the actor
grammar.formation: 伺う → 伺います / 伺ってもよろしいでしょうか; suitable お/ご + verb stem + いただけますか requests the other person’s act.
grammar.explanation: 伺う can humbly mean asking, hearing or visiting a respected recipient. Here the applicant asks about training. ご説明いただけますか asks the interviewer to explain; ご説明いたします says the applicant will explain. Both can be polite, but their actors differ. Use the question and the following answer to determine who acts.
grammar.example: 研修について伺ってもよろしいでしょうか。
grammar.translation: May I ask about the training?

examples.ja: {研修|けんしゅう}について{伺|うかが}ってもよろしいでしょうか。
examples.en: May I ask about the training?

examples.ja: もう{少|すこ}し{詳|くわ}しくご{説明|せつめい}いただけますか。
examples.en: Could you explain in a little more detail?

examples.ja: {資料|しりょう}を{拝見|はいけん}しました。
examples.en: I’ve looked at the materials.

grammar.mistake: 伺う is not the respectful form for the interviewer’s own question. Do not treat two valid request lengths as a right/wrong contrast.

grammar.title: Answer the follow-up with an action and its result
grammar.formation: Conclusion → specific past action → result → future application; tense distinguishes completed experience from a planned contribution.
grammar.explanation: This is a discourse strategy, not a grammatical suffix or guaranteed interview formula. If asked what you changed, identify the changed item and the check that followed. If asked what you want to do, state an intention rather than claiming an appointment or achievement. A sincere short answer with useful detail is better than a list of unrelated strengths.
grammar.example: 地図の字を大きくして、森さんに確認していただきました。
grammar.translation: I enlarged the map lettering and had Mori-san check it.

examples.ja: {地図|ちず}の{字|じ}を{大|おお}きくして、{森|もり}さんに{確認|かくにん}していただきました。
examples.en: I enlarged the map lettering and had Mori-san check it.

examples.ja: {実習|じっしゅう}の{経験|けいけん}を{案内|あんない}の{作成|さくせい}に{役立|やくだ}てたいです。
examples.en: I’d like to use my internship experience in making brochures.

examples.ja: {結果|けっか}は{来週|らいしゅう}の{金曜日|きんようび}までに{届|とど}く{予定|よてい}です。
examples.en: The result is due by next Friday.

grammar.mistake: A positive interview response or an explanation of training does not itself mean you have been hired.

lines.line: ご{自分|じぶん}の{強|つよ}みは、どんな{点|てん}だと{思|おも}いますか。
lines.romaji: Gojibun no tsuyomi wa, donna ten da to omoimasu ka.
lines.meaning: What do you think is your strength?

lines.speaker: You
lines.line: {分|わ}からない{点|てん}を{残|のこ}さず、{相手|あいて}に{確認|かくにん}することです。
lines.romaji: Wakaranai ten o nokosazu, aite ni kakunin suru koto desu.
lines.meaning: Checking with the other person rather than leaving something unclear.

lines.speaker: Ishikawa
lines.line: うまくいかなかったこともありますか。
lines.romaji: Umaku ikanakatta koto mo arimasu ka.
lines.meaning: Has anything not gone well?

lines.speaker: You
lines.line: はい。{先方|せんぽう}へ{送|おく}ったメールで、{曜日|ようび}を{書|か}き{間違|まちが}えました。
lines.romaji: Hai. Senpō e okutta mēru de, yōbi o kakimachigaemashita.
lines.meaning: Yes. I wrote the wrong weekday in an email to the client.

lines.speaker: Ishikawa
lines.line: その{時|とき}は、どう{対応|たいおう}しましたか。
lines.romaji: Sono toki wa, dō taiō shimashita ka.
lines.meaning: How did you respond then?

lines.speaker: You
lines.line: {日付|ひづけ}と{曜日|ようび}を{確認|かくにん}して、メールを{再送|さいそう}しました。{今|いま}は、{送|おく}る{前|まえ}に{予定表|よていひょう}で{確認|かくにん}しています。
lines.romaji: Hizuke to yōbi o kakunin shite, mēru o saisō shimashita. Ima wa, okuru mae ni yoteihyō de kakunin shite imasu.
lines.meaning: I checked the date and weekday and resent the email. Now I check the schedule before sending.

lines.speaker: Ishikawa
lines.line: {弱|よわ}みについてはいかがですか。
lines.romaji: Yowami ni tsuite wa ikaga desu ka.
lines.meaning: And what about a weakness?

lines.speaker: You
lines.line: {緊張|きんちょう}すると、{説明|せつめい}が{長|なが}くなることです。{実習|じっしゅう}の{発表|はっぴょう}でも、{方法|ほうほう}の{説明|せつめい}を{直|なお}しました。
lines.romaji: Kinchō suru to, setsumei ga nagaku naru koto desu. Jisshū no happyō de mo, hōhō no setsumei o naoshimashita.
lines.meaning: My explanations get long when I’m nervous. I revised the method explanation in my internship presentation too.

lines.speaker: Ishikawa
lines.line: {今|いま}は、どんな{練習|れんしゅう}をしていますか。
lines.romaji: Ima wa, donna renshū o shite imasu ka.
lines.meaning: How are you practising now?

lines.speaker: You
lines.line: {先|さき}に{結論|けつろん}を{伝|つた}え、{一|ひと}つの{文|ぶん}に{情報|じょうほう}を{入|い}れすぎないようにしています。
lines.romaji: Saki ni ketsuron o tsutae, hitotsu no bun ni jōhō o iresuginai yō ni shite imasu.
lines.meaning: I give the main point first and try not to put too much information in one sentence.

lines.speaker: Ishikawa
lines.line: ありがとうございます。{最後|さいご}に、{何|なに}かご{質問|しつもん}はありますか。
lines.romaji: Arigatō gozaimasu. Saigo ni, nanika goshitsumon wa arimasu ka.
lines.meaning: Thank you. Finally, do you have any questions?

lines.speaker: You
lines.line: {入社|にゅうしゃ}{後|ご}の{研修|けんしゅう}について{伺|うかが}ってもよろしいでしょうか。
lines.romaji: Nyūsha go no kenshū ni tsuite ukagatte mo yoroshii deshō ka.
lines.meaning: May I ask about training after joining?

lines.speaker: Ishikawa
lines.line: {最初|さいしょ}の{一|いっ}か{月|げつ}は{基本|きほん}を{学|まな}び、その{後|あと}は{先輩|せんぱい}と{仕事|しごと}をします。{選考|せんこう}の{結果|けっか}は{来週|らいしゅう}の{金曜日|きんようび}までにメールでお{知|し}らせします。
lines.romaji: Saisho no ikkagetsu wa kihon o manabi, sono ato wa senpai to shigoto o shimasu. Senkō no kekka wa raishū no kin’yōbi made ni mēru de oshirase shimasu.
lines.meaning: You learn the basics in the first month, then work with a senior colleague. We’ll email the selection result by next Friday.

lines.speaker: You
lines.line: {承知|しょうち}しました。ご{連絡|れんらく}をお{待|ま}ちしております。{本日|ほんじつ}はありがとうございました。
lines.romaji: Shōchi shimashita. Gorenraku o omachi shite orimasu. Honjitsu wa arigatō gozaimashita.
lines.meaning: Understood. I’ll wait for your message. Thank you for meeting me today.

grammar: applicant action versus interviewer action in keigo
watch.prompt: Optionally listen to a short interview or a rehearsal you already have. Identify the question, the specific action supporting the answer, and the stated next step. Keep notes about the content rather than counting honourifics.

recycling.reason: The capstone retrieves actual earlier brochure/presentation/call work and useful recent terms; unrelated concert, regional and opinion words are not forced into an interview. Supplementary employment words belong in the meet lists, not every answer.

exercises.prompt: What work does Bao want to do?
options: Make information easy for its users to understand
Choose the company’s entire hiring policy
Guarantee a sales increase already achieved
exercises.explain: Bao wants to make useful clear information and applies the reader-perspective checking habit. No hiring or sales result is claimed.

exercises.prompt: What did Bao change in the four-page brochure?
options: The company name on every page
The lettering on the final map
exercises.explain: Bao enlarged the lettering on the last map; address and date checks are follow-up work.

exercises.prompt: What did Bao check besides the appearance?
options: The venue address and date and time
exercises.explain: The map could be readable while a wrong address still misleads visitors; no actual wrong address is claimed.

exercises.prompt: Choose a deferential way for Bao to state their own name to the interviewer.
exercises.line: バオと{言|い}います。
options: バオとおっしゃいます。
バオをご{覧|らん}になります。
exercises.explain: 申します names the speaker deferentially. The other forms refer respectfully to another person saying or looking.
exercises.context: Choose a deferential way for Bao to state their own name to the interviewer.
The applicant offers to explain their own reason for applying.
exercises.line: {志望|しぼう}した{理由|りゆう}をご{説明|せつめい}＿＿。
exercises.explain: ご説明いたします describes the applicant’s explanation. なさいます honours another actor; ください asks someone else.

exercises.prompt: Which company does the applicant refer to here?
exercises.line: {御社|おんしゃ}で{働|はたら}きたいと{考|かんが}えております。
options: A company the applicant already owns
exercises.explain: 御社 is the spoken courteous reference to the addressee’s company, not proof of employment.

exercises.prompt: Which experience supports Bao’s reason for applying?
options: Revising an actual brochure for its readers
Receiving an offer before the interview
exercises.explain: The map and contents checks connect with making useful materials.

exercises.prompt: Why did Bao leave out a claim that sales increased?
options: The company forbids all numerical details
The brochure never contained a map
exercises.explain: Bao does not include a result that has not been confirmed; this is not a universal ban on sales figures.

exercises.prompt: Which references were prepared for the two media?
options: 御社 only in the application and 貴社 only in the interview
弊社 for both references to the interviewer’s company
貴社 in the application and 御社 in the interview
exercises.explain: The preparation note names the written and spoken choices explicitly.

exercises.prompt: What is true before the interview?
options: There is no job offer yet
Bao has already joined as a regular employee
exercises.explain: 内定はまだ出ていない explicitly keeps the result open.

exercises.prompt: What did Bao do after writing the wrong weekday?
options: Waited for the selection result without correcting it
Checked the date and weekday and resent the corrected email
Changed the client’s appointment without asking
exercises.explain: The revised email repairs the error; the later habit is checking the schedule before sending.

exercises.prompt: How is Bao working on explanations that become long?
options: Speak without any pauses until the listener leaves
Give the main point first and limit information in each sentence
exercises.explain: Bao practices 結論 first and avoids putting too much into one sentence.

exercises.prompt: What sequence does Ishikawa describe for new employees?
options: A month of basics, then working with a senior colleague
Immediate solo management of the whole company
A confirmed department assignment before selection
exercises.explain: Ishikawa explains training after entry. It does not announce Bao’s hiring.

exercises.prompt: Who asks in this line?
exercises.line: {研修|けんしゅう}について{伺|うかが}ってもよろしいでしょうか。
options: The interviewer, humbly ordering the applicant to leave
exercises.explain: Here 伺う is the applicant’s humble question; it does not honour the interviewer as action-doer.

exercises.prompt: Choose the request asking the interviewer to explain the duties.
exercises.line: {職務|しょくむ}について、もう{少|すこ}し{説明|せつめい}してください。
options: もう{少|すこ}しご{説明|せつめい}いたします。
これ{以上|いじょう}{説明|せつめい}しないでください。
もう{少|すこ}しご{説明|せつめい}いただけますか。
exercises.explain: いただけますか requests the interviewer’s act. いたします offers the speaker’s act, and the last choice asks them not to explain.
exercises.context: Choose the request asking the interviewer to explain the duties.

exercises.prompt: Build the supplied closing sentence saying you will wait for contact.
exercises.explain: This is the supplied deferential closing, not the only natural wording and not unrestricted production.
exercises.meaning: Constrained recall: I will wait for your message.

exercises.prompt: What is the status of the selection result?
options: It is still expected by next Friday by email
It arrived with this thank-you email
exercises.explain: The writer acknowledges a promised notification and waits; the email is thanks, not an offer.

exercises.prompt: Which training sequence did Bao learn about?
options: Start immediately alone with no basic training
First learn the basics, then work with a senior colleague
Receive a specific department assignment in this thank-you email
exercises.explain: The second paragraph repeats the one-month basics followed by work with a senior colleague. Neither the interview nor this email specifies a department assignment.

exercises.prompt: Why is the résumé not attached to this email?
options: Ishikawa requested deletion of all documents
exercises.explain: すでに提出しております…添付しておりません gives the reason directly.

exercises.prompt: Which habits will Bao continue?
options: Check the schedule and practice giving the conclusion first
Assume a department has already been selected
List every supplementary vocabulary word in each answer
exercises.explain: The third paragraph names both concrete practices, not a vocabulary quota.

grammar.title: A gesture described as almost doing something
grammar.formation: Negative verb stem (remove ない) + んばかりに + predicate; + んばかりの + noun; + んばかりだ. する → せんばかり.
grammar.explanation: This expressive description presents an appearance close to an action, often figuratively. 言わんばかりの眼差し describes a look as if it said something; it does not report a spoken quotation. に connects the description to an action, while の attaches it to a noun. It fits narration or a deliberately expressive recollection more readily than every ordinary turn. Usually describe an observed scene; do not turn it into a claim that you know someone’s actual thoughts.
grammar.example: 彼は「まだ待って」と言わんばかりに手を振った。
grammar.translation: He waved his hand as if to say, “Wait a little longer.”

examples.ja: {彼|かれ}は「まだ{待|ま}って」と{言|い}わんばかりに{手|て}を{振|ふ}った。
examples.en: He waved his hand as if to say, “Wait a little longer.”

examples.ja: {窓|まど}の{外|そと}には{溢|あふ}れんばかりの{光|ひかり}が{広|ひろ}がっていた。
examples.en: Outside the window, light seemed to overflow.

examples.ja: {娘|むすめ}は{跳|と}び{上|あ}がらんばかりに{喜|よろこ}んだ。
examples.en: The daughter was so delighted she looked ready to jump for joy.

grammar.mistake: Remove ない before adding ん; する uses せん, not しん. A narrated appearance does not establish that the action actually happened.

grammar.title: An obstacle does not stop the action
grammar.formation: Obstacle noun + をものともせず（に） + an action continued despite it.
grammar.explanation: The expression gives the action a determined, often admiring or dramatic tone: a person keeps going despite an obstacle. It is stronger than simply saying there was difficulty. Here friends quote a storm scene from a story, then talk normally about what the character did. Do not read the phrase alone as proof that the action succeeded. The original fiction gives the concrete result separately.
grammar.example: 彼女は反対をものともせず、原稿を書き続けた。
grammar.translation: She kept writing her manuscript despite the opposition.

examples.ja: {彼女|かのじょ}は{反対|はんたい}をものともせず、{原稿|げんこう}を{書|か}き{続|つづ}けた。
examples.en: She kept writing her manuscript despite the opposition.

examples.ja: {主人公|しゅじんこう}は{寒|さむ}さをものともせず、{橋|はし}まで{歩|ある}いた。
examples.en: The protagonist walked as far as the bridge despite the cold.

examples.ja: {彼|かれ}は{何度|なんど}もの{失敗|しっぱい}をものともせずに{練習|れんしゅう}を{続|つづ}けた。
examples.en: He kept practicing despite repeated failures.

grammar.mistake: Use a noun naming the obstacle. The narrator gives the viewpoint; the following clauses establish the action and result.

grammar.title: A valued quality tied to its particular source
grammar.formation: Noun + ならではの + noun; Noun + ならではだ when the quality is already identified.
grammar.explanation: This presents something as a characteristic or distinctive strength of that person, material or experience, commonly with appreciative evaluation. In this unit, 手書きならではの味わい is the writer’s response to marks on a fictional letter. It does not claim that every handwritten work is superior to a screen, or that a geographic feature cannot exist elsewhere. The noun after の names the valued quality.

grammar.title: Not even one: a strong negative boundary
grammar.formation: One + counter / a minimal quantity + たりとも + negative or prohibition. Examples: 一字たりとも消さない; 一瞬たりとも忘れない.
grammar.explanation: This strongly excludes even the smallest named amount. It is formal or deliberately emphatic, rather than an everyday replacement for every も. The editor’s 一字たりとも消さない expresses a vow about an original letter; it is not a ban on revising the new story. The following predicate supplies the negative boundary. paragraphs: {原稿|げんこう}を{書|か}き{始|はじ}めた{時|とき}、{私|わたし}は{主人公|しゅじんこう}の{気持|きも}ちを{説明|せつめい}すれば{読者|どくしゃ}に{伝|つた}わると{思|おも}っていた。「{不安|ふあん}だった」「{父|ちち}を{理解|りかい}できなかった」「それでも{帰|かえ}りたかった」と、{同|おな}じ{場面|ばめん}に{三|みっ}つの{説明|せつめい}を{置|お}いた。{声|こえ}に{出|だ}して{読|よ}むと、{息|いき}をつく{場所|ばしょ}がなくなった。{窓|まど}の{明|あ}かりも、{濡|ぬ}れた{紙袋|かみぶくろ}も、{説明|せつめい}の{後|うし}ろに{隠|かく}れていた。そこで、{説明|せつめい}を{二|ふた}つ{消|け}し、{残|のこ}った{一|ひと}つも{短|みじか}くした。{読者|どくしゃ}が{見|み}られる{動作|どうさ}を{先|さき}に{置|お}くようにしたのである。

{次|つぎ}に{直|なお}したのは{橋|はし}の{場面|ばめん}だ。「{風|かぜ}をものともせず」という{一行|いちぎょう}は、{娘|むすめ}のひたむきな{動|うご}きを{描|えが}く。しかし、{走|はし}り{続|つづ}けて{家|いえ}に{着|つ}く{話|はなし}にはしなかった。{足元|あしもと}を{見|み}て、{風|かぜ}が{弱|よわ}くなるのを{待|ま}つ。{戻|もど}りたいという{気持|きも}ちと、{少|すこ}し{待|ま}つという{行動|こうどう}は{両立|りょうりつ}する。{物語|ものがたり}の{速度|そくど}を{上|あ}げることだけが、{強|つよ}い{決意|けつい}の{描写|びょうしゃ}ではない。{途中|とちゅう}で{立|た}ち{止|ど}まる{時間|じかん}にも、その{人|ひと}の{持|も}ち{味|あじ}が{出|で}る。ミサキが「{息|いき}を{止|と}めちゃった」と{言|い}ったのは、その{短|みじか}い{間|ま}だった。

{便|たよ}りの{字|じ}には{大小|だいしょう}の{違|ちが}いを{残|のこ}した。{美|うつく}しい{装丁|そうてい}の{冊子|さっし}にする{予定|よてい}でも、{父|ちち}の{字|じ}を{全部|ぜんぶ}{同|おな}じ{形|かたち}に{直|なお}すと、{別|べつ}の{声|こえ}になってしまう{気|き}がしたからだ。{手書|てが}きならではの{味|あじ}わいを{紙面|しめん}に{残|のこ}すため、{文字|もじ}の{大|おお}きさを{少|すこ}しだけ{変|か}えた。{画面|がめん}で{読|よ}む{人|ひと}にも{見|み}えるように、{薄|うす}い{色|いろ}ではなく、はっきりした{線|せん}を{選|えら}んだ。{紙|かみ}と{画面|がめん}のどちらにも{読者|どくしゃ}がいる。{素材|そざい}を{選|えら}ぶ{楽|たの}しさと、{字|じ}を{読|よ}めるようにする{工夫|くふう}は、{別々|べつべつ}に{考|かんが}えた。

grammar: a quoted expressive description versus an actual spoken line
minimal quantity with a negative predicate
watch.prompt: Optionally listen to a short narration you already have. Note whether a quoted line was spoken or only suggested, what the character actually did, and one expressive phrase. No media upload or independent comprehension score is required.

recycling.reason: The first N1 literary unit reuses only actual recent events: Bao’s Friday offer follows the pending interview and next month starts with training. Handwritten material and ordinary friend conversation are not padded with job/slang/dialect headwords.

exercises.prompt: When does the daughter read the letter?
options: The next morning, after returning to the seaside house
At the doorway before she leaves
exercises.explain: Hana says 翌朝, and Ren checks that she has not read it on the rainy night.

exercises.prompt: What first confuses Ren about the doorway scene?
options: He thinks the daughter cannot see the light
He thinks the father shouted a line that was only suggested by a gesture
He thinks the father has read the daughter’s letter
exercises.explain: Ren rereads because he takes 行くな as a shout. Hana says 叫んでない and explains the appearance.

exercises.prompt: Which phrase does Hana consider keeping to make the viewpoint clear?
options: {父|ちち}は{全|すべ}て{説明|せつめい}した
{便|たよ}りはすでに{届|とど}いた
{娘|むすめ}にはそう{見|み}えた
exercises.explain: It identifies how the daughter sees the gesture, rather than reporting the father’s spoken words.

exercises.prompt: Complete the adverbial attachment describing how he waved.
exercises.line: {彼|かれ}は「{待|ま}って」と{言|い}わんばかり＿＿{手|て}を{振|ふ}った。
exercises.explain: に links the expressive appearance to the action 手を振った. の needs a following noun.

exercises.prompt: Choose the modifier for the noun 光景: “a scene that seems to overflow with light.”
exercises.line: {光|ひかり}が{溢|あふ}れんばかり＿＿{光景|こうけい}
exercises.explain: The immediate noun needs の. This is an explicit attachment task, not a choice between multiple valid full descriptions.

exercises.prompt: What does this narrated description establish?
exercises.line: {彼|かれ}は「{帰|かえ}って」と{言|い}わんばかりの{眼差|まなざ}しを{向|む}けた。
options: The exact words 帰って were definitely spoken aloud
The narrator describes a look as if it conveyed “Go home”
exercises.explain: The described appearance neither establishes an audible quotation nor the other person’s subsequent action.

exercises.prompt: What does the daughter do before crossing?
options: Wait for the wind to ease and check her footing
Run without looking at the boards
Read the letter aloud to Misaki
exercises.explain: Hana says she stops before the bridge, waits, and watches her footing. The strong phrase does not erase those actions.

exercises.prompt: Why can the writing still be read the next morning?
options: The letter is rewritten on a phone
The daughter wraps the paper bag in a clear bag
The father replaces it with a printed copy
exercises.explain: Hana describes the extra bag, and Misaki links it to the writing remaining readable.

exercises.prompt: Choose the supplied obstacle expression before the continued action.
exercises.line: {反対|はんたい}＿＿、{彼女|かのじょ}は{書|か}き{続|つづ}けた。
exercises.explain: Noun + をものともせず connects the named obstacle to the action that goes on despite it.

exercises.prompt: Build the supplied appreciative description of handwriting.
exercises.meaning: There is a distinctive handwritten charm.
exercises.explain: The source noun precedes ならではの and the valued quality follows it. This constrained target is not the only possible compliment.

exercises.prompt: Why does the daughter head back to the house?
options: To think again about her hurry in the light of the house
To return an unwanted letter and leave immediately
To ask the father to write an address before she can travel
exercises.explain: The bridge paragraph distinguishes returning the letter from returning to think again about what she was rushing towards.

exercises.prompt: What does the letter offer the daughter?
options: A fixed destination and departure day
A place she can return to if she has trouble
An order that she must never leave the house
exercises.explain: The morning paragraph says it is not a letter deciding where she must go; it tells her there is a place to come back to.

exercises.prompt: Which change occurs between the first doorway scene and the final window scene?
options: The father finally shouts 行くな
The daughter responds with a wave and a spoken question
exercises.explain: She opens the window, waves back and asks about breakfast. Departure is still undecided.

exercises.prompt: What new work arrangement does Bao describe?
options: An offer received on Friday, entry next month, and a month of training
An unresolved result due after the booklet is printed
exercises.explain: This later scene explicitly confirms Friday’s offer and next month’s entry; it does not rewrite the earlier interview’s pending status.

exercises.prompt: Which document is covered by Ren’s “not even one character” remark?
options: Every draft Hana will ever write
The father’s letter inside the story
exercises.explain: Hana identifies the fictional father’s letter and then agrees to shorten the new explanatory paragraph.

exercises.prompt: Complete the strong negative vow about the entrusted manuscript.
exercises.line: {預|あず}かった{原稿|げんこう}は{一枚|いちまい}たりとも＿＿。
exercises.explain: The negative predicate gives this minimum-unit vow its meaning. Losing it and wanting to lose it contradict the stated vow.

exercises.prompt: Why does Hana keep 娘にはそう見えた?
options: To show the daughter’s viewpoint without revealing the father’s message early
To establish that the father shouted the exact words
To move the letter-reading scene to the beginning
exercises.explain: The second paragraph explains viewpoint and the order in which the letter’s words reach both daughter and reader.

exercises.prompt: How does the writer treat paper and screen readers?
options: She makes all handwriting identical and uses a very pale colour
She keeps varied lettering and clear lines readable for both
She denies that anyone reads on screens
exercises.explain: The material paragraph separates enjoyment of materials from making the lettering readable; it explicitly considers screen readers.

exercises.prompt: What is done with the words removed from the new draft?
options: They are erased from the fictional father’s letter
They are sent as Bao’s interview answer
They are kept on another sheet for a later draft
exercises.explain: The writer records the removed words separately; preserving the letter and revising the surrounding draft are different decisions.

exercises.prompt: Which feedback does Hana plan to ask for at the meetup?
options: Where readers took a breath or reread, and what they waited for before the letter opened
Only the colour of the paper, without reading aloud
A vote to forbid any further editing
exercises.explain: The closing paragraph asks about concrete reading behaviour rather than relying only on a broad 分かった response.

grammar.title: A strong judgement against a role’s standard
grammar.formation: Verb dictionary form + まじき + noun; frequent fixed frame: role noun + にあるまじき + 行為. する may take すまじき in marked written language.
grammar.explanation: まじき condemns conduct as unacceptable for a position or standard. It is strong, formal and usually modifies a noun. 編集者にあるまじき行為 means conduct unworthy of an editor, not conduct that is physically impossible. In this unit friends discuss a quoted editorial after a fabricated interview, then distinguish it from a corrected date error. This is recognition and contextual interpretation, not a routine label to apply to someone who makes a mistake.
grammar.example: 発言を勝手に作るのは、取材者にあるまじき行為だ。
grammar.translation: Inventing someone’s remarks is conduct unworthy of an interviewer.

examples.ja: {発言|はつげん}を{勝|か}{手|て}に{作|つく}るのは、{取材者|しゅざいしゃ}にあるまじき{行為|こうい}だ。
examples.en: Inventing someone’s remarks is conduct unworthy of an interviewer.

examples.ja: {彼|かれ}は「{許|ゆる}すまじき{不正|ふせい}」と{書|か}き、{記録|きろく}を{示|しめ}した。
examples.en: He called it “unacceptable misconduct” and presented the records.

examples.ja: {責任者|せきにんしゃ}にあるまじき{軽率|けいそつ}な{発言|はつげん}だった。
examples.en: It was a careless remark unworthy of the person responsible.

grammar.mistake: The standard belongs to a stated role or context. Do not confuse a strong moral judgement with factual impossibility, or treat every error as deliberate misconduct.

grammar.title: A new scale changes what is needed
grammar.formation: Noun / verb dictionary form + ともなると or ともなれば + an expected judgement or consequence.
grammar.explanation: The speaker treats a new role, scale or stage as significant and explains what is expected at that point. A larger event may need a different staffing plan; the scene gives its actual conditions. The result is an assessment, not an unavoidable rule about every group of that size. A direct wish or decision such as 私が受付をしたい does not give the taught consequent judgement.
grammar.example: 二百人の会ともなると、受付を一人には任せられない。
grammar.translation: For a gathering of two hundred, one person can’t handle reception alone.

examples.ja: {二百人|にひゃくにん}の{会|かい}ともなると、{受付|うけつけ}を{一人|ひとり}には{任|まか}せられない。
examples.en: For a gathering of two hundred, one person can’t handle reception alone.

examples.ja: {責任者|せきにんしゃ}ともなると、{自分|じぶん}の{作業|さぎょう}だけ{見|み}ていればいいわけではない。
examples.en: As the person responsible, you can’t just watch your own work.

examples.ja: {毎月|まいつき}{開|あ}くともなると、{引|ひ}き{継|つ}ぎの{方法|ほうほう}も{必要|ひつよう}になる。
examples.en: If we’re going to hold it every month, we also need a way to hand things over.

grammar.mistake: Identify the consequential assessment. Do not infer a universally required team size from one event’s planning judgement.

grammar.title: Pick out the most troubling case
grammar.formation: A noun naming one case + に至っては + the especially striking result, after the wider comparison is established.
grammar.explanation: The expression singles out a conspicuous, usually negative case. Here the text contains date and name errors, and the map even reverses entry and exit. に至っては highlights that map as the worst example in this draft. It differs from に至って meaning reaching a stage or only at that stage, and に至っても meaning even after reaching it.
grammar.example: 名前にも誤りがあり、案内図に至っては入口と出口が逆だった。
grammar.translation: The names had errors too; as for the map, even the entrance and exit were reversed.

examples.ja: {名前|なまえ}にも{誤|あやま}りがあり、{案内図|あんないず}に{至|いた}っては{入口|いりぐち}と{出口|でぐち}が{逆|ぎゃく}だった。
examples.en: The names had errors too; as for the map, even the entrance and exit were reversed.

examples.ja: {返信|へんしん}が{遅|おそ}れ、{最後|さいご}の{一件|いっけん}に{至|いた}っては{連絡先|れんらくさき}も{違|ちが}っていた。
examples.en: Replies were late, and the last one even had the wrong contact details.

examples.ja: {紙面|しめん}には{小|ちい}さな{誤記|ごき}が{残|のこ}り、{表紙|ひょうし}に{至|いた}っては{開催日|かいさいび}が{古|ふる}いままだった。
examples.en: Small errors remained inside, and even the cover still carried the old event date.

grammar.mistake: Supply the comparison that makes this particular case extreme. The ending は is part of the taught frame; do not substitute に至っても without changing the meaning.

grammar.title: A formal boundary, or a formal means
grammar.formation: Time/event noun + をもって（formal polite をもちまして） for the closing boundary here; means noun + をもって for formal procedure.
grammar.explanation: The notice closes exhibition viewing at six but new applications at five. The noun before をもって sets that specific boundary. 書面をもって通知する specifies written notice as the formal means, not a deadline. 普通のメールで送る is often more natural in everyday conversation. This unit teaches these closing and means uses; it does not claim every starting-date use is impossible.
grammar.example: 四月二十日午後六時をもって、展示を終了します。
grammar.translation: The exhibition will close at six p.m. on April twentieth.

examples.ja: {四月|しがつ}{二十日|はつか}{午後|ごご}{六時|ろくじ}をもって、{展示|てんじ}を{終了|しゅうりょう}します。
examples.en: The exhibition will close at six p.m. on April twentieth.

examples.ja: {変更|へんこう}した{時刻|じこく}は、{書面|しょめん}をもって{申込者|もうしこみしゃ}に{通知|つうち}します。
examples.en: We’ll notify applicants of the changed time in writing.

examples.ja: {以上|いじょう}をもちまして、{閉会|へいかい}の{挨拶|あいさつ}といたします。
examples.en: With that, I conclude these closing remarks.

grammar.mistake: Read the noun and the whole predicate: an ending boundary is different from a means of notification. The formal means use does not require a seal unless the actual procedure says so.

dialogues.title: Two incidents, two people

lines.speaker: Ren
lines.line: ハナ、{会報|かいほう}のこの{論評|ろんぴょう}、かなり{強|つよ}い{言|い}い{方|かた}だね。
lines.romaji: Hana, kaihō no kono ronpyō, kanari tsuyoi iikata da ne.
lines.meaning: Hana, this newsletter editorial uses pretty strong language.

lines.speaker: Hana
lines.line: 「{編集者|へんしゅうしゃ}にあるまじき{行為|こうい}」のところ？
lines.romaji: Henshūsha ni aru majiki kōi no tokoro?
lines.meaning: The bit about “conduct unworthy of an editor”?

lines.speaker: Ren
lines.line: うん。{何|なに}をしたんだっけ。
lines.romaji: Un. Nani o shita n dakke.
lines.meaning: Yeah. What did they do again?

lines.speaker: Hana
lines.line: {取材|しゅざい}してない{人|ひと}の{発言|はつげん}を{作|つく}って、{本人|ほんにん}の{言葉|ことば}として{載|の}せたんだって。
lines.romaji: Shuzai shitenai hito no hatsugen o tsukutte, honnin no kotoba to shite noseta n datte.
lines.meaning: Apparently they made up remarks from someone they hadn’t interviewed and printed them as that person’s words.

lines.speaker: Ren
lines.line: それはまずい。{日付|ひづけ}を{間違|まちが}えた{話|はなし}とは{別|べつ}なんだ。
lines.romaji: Sore wa mazui. Hizuke o machigaeta hanashi to wa betsu nan da.
lines.meaning: That’s bad. So it’s a separate incident from the wrong date.

lines.speaker: Hana
lines.line: そう。{日付|ひづけ}の{方|ほう}は{訂正欄|ていせいらん}に、{直|なお}した{日|ひ}と{理由|りゆう}が{出|で}てる。
lines.romaji: Sō. Hizuke no hō wa teiseiran ni, naoshita hi to riyū ga deteru.

readings.title: Six for the exhibition; five for applications
paragraphs: {四月|しがつ}{二十日|はつか}の{展示会|てんじかい}は、{午後|ごご}{六時|ろくじ}をもって{終了|しゅうりょう}した。{前日|ぜんじつ}に{届|とど}いた{通知|つうち}には、{以前|いぜん}の{案内|あんない}で{午後|ごご}{五時|ごじ}としていた{展示|てんじ}の{終了時刻|しゅうりょうじこく}を、{一時間|いちじかん}{遅|おそ}くすると{書|か}かれていた。{変更|へんこう}は{展示|てんじ}を{見|み}る{人|ひと}にも{掲示板|けいじばん}で{伝|つた}えた。{一方|いっぽう}、{次回|じかい}の{展示|てんじ}の{申|もう}し{込|こ}みを{受|う}け{付|つ}けるのは{午後|ごご}{五時|ごじ}までで、この{時刻|じこく}は{変|か}わらなかった。{五時|ごじ}を{過|す}ぎても{会場|かいじょう}には{人|ひと}が{残|のこ}っていたが、{申|もう}し{込|こ}みの{受付|うけつけ}は{閉|と}じ、{案内係|あんないがかり}が{展示|てんじ}の{見方|みかた}を{説明|せつめい}していた。

{閉会|へいかい}の{挨拶|あいさつ}をするハナは、{二種類|にしゅるい}の{終了時刻|しゅうりょうじこく}を{間違|まちが}えないよう、{原稿|げんこう}の{数字|すうじ}に{線|せん}を{引|ひ}いた。{会場|かいじょう}の{代表|だいひょう}{者|しゃ}からは、{変更|へんこう}した{時刻|じこく}を{書面|しょめん}をもって{申込者|もうしこみしゃ}に{通知|つうち}するよう{依頼|いらい}されていた。{書面|しょめん}という{手段|しゅだん}を{選|えら}んだのは、{申込者|もうしこみしゃ}が{自分|じぶん}の{展示|てんじ}をいつまで{出|だ}しておけるか、{後|あと}で{読|よ}み{直|なお}せるようにするためだった。{通知|つうち}には{会場|かいじょう}の{代表|だいひょう}{者|しゃ}の{名前|なまえ}と{連絡先|れんらくさき}を{載|の}せた。この{通知|つうち}では{捺印|なついん}を{求|もと}める{手順|てじゅん}はなく、{受|う}け{取|と}った{人|ひと}にも{印|いん}を{押|お}して{返|かえ}すようには{頼|たの}まなかった。

{前年|ぜんねん}は{五十人|ごじゅうにん}ほどの{小|ちい}さな{会|かい}だった。{今年|ことし}は{二百人|にひゃくにん}まで{入|い}れる{会場|かいじょう}を{使|つか}い、{入口|いりぐち}と{案内|あんない}にそれぞれ{二人|ふたり}を{置|お}いた。{二百人|にひゃくにん}の{会|かい}ともなると、{担当者|たんとうしゃ}が{休|やす}む{順番|じゅんばん}も{決|き}めておく{必要|ひつよう}があった。{開始前|かいしまえ}、{全員|ぜんいん}が{案内図|あんないず}を{持|も}って{会場|かいじょう}を{歩|ある}いた。{図|ず}の{入口|いりぐち}と{出口|でぐち}が{逆|ぎゃく}だったため、{書|か}き{直|なお}した{二度目|にどめ}の{図|ず}で{確|たし}かめたのである。{紙面|しめん}の{体裁|ていさい}を{整|ととの}えるだけでは、{実際|じっさい}の{人|ひと}の{移動|いどう}までは{分|わ}からなかった。

{午後|ごご}{四時台|よじだい}には、{来場者|らいじょうしゃ}が{入口側|いりぐちがわ}に{集|あつ}まった。{案内係|あんないがかり}は{出口側|でぐちがわ}にも{展示|てんじ}が{続|つづ}いていることを{伝|つた}え、{列|れつ}の{向|む}きを{変|か}えた。ハナは{原稿|げんこう}を{見|み}ながら{入口|いりぐち}に{立|た}つのをやめ、{挨拶|あいさつ}の{準備|じゅんび}を{別|べつ}の{机|つくえ}で{行|おこな}った。そこに{立|た}ったままでは、{来場者|らいじょうしゃ}の{通|とお}り{道|みち}を{狭|せま}くしてしまうからだ。{責任者|せきにんしゃ}ともなると、{自分|じぶん}が{早|はや}く{準備|じゅんび}できる{場所|ばしょ}だけでなく、{他|ほか}の{人|ひと}がどこを{通|とお}るかも{考|かんが}えなければならないと{感|かん}じた。

{六時|ろくじ}の{十五分|じゅうごふん}{前|まえ}、ハナは{最後|さいご}の{案内|あんない}を{短|みじか}く{読|よ}んだ。{残|のこ}り{十五分|じゅうごふん}で{展示|てんじ}を{見終|みお}えてほしいことと、{忘|わす}れ{物|もの}の{問|と}い{合|あ}わせ{先|さき}を{伝|つた}えた。{正式|せいしき}な{閉会式|へいかいしき}のような{長|なが}い{祝辞|しゅくじ}は{用意|ようい}しなかった。{今回|こんかい}の{趣旨|しゅし}は、{出|だ}した{作品|さくひん}を{見|み}ながら{互|たが}いに{話|はな}すことで、{代表|だいひょう}{者|しゃ}の{話|はなし}を{長|なが}く{聞|き}くことではなかったからである。{六時|ろくじ}には{来場者|らいじょうしゃ}にお{礼|れい}を{述|の}べ、{展示|てんじ}を{終了|しゅうりょう}した。{続|つづ}く{片付|かたづ}けは{関係者|かんけいしゃ}だけで{行|おこな}った。

{翌日|よくじつ}、ハナは{会|かい}の{顛末|てんまつ}を{短|みじか}い{記録|きろく}にした。{古|ふる}い{日付|ひづけ}を{見|み}た{人|ひと}への{通知|つうち}、{案内図|あんないず}の{入|い}れ{替|か}え、{休|やす}む{順番|じゅんばん}、{入口|いりぐち}の{混雑|こんざつ}への{対処|たいしょ}を{順|じゅん}に{書|か}いた。{挨拶|あいさつ}では「{以上|いじょう}をもちまして、{閉会|へいかい}の{挨拶|あいさつ}といたします」と{言|い}ったが、それで{後|あと}の{仕事|しごと}まで{終|お}わるわけではない。{記録|きろく}を{残|のこ}し、{借|か}りた{物|もの}を{返|かえ}し、{来年|らいねん}の{担当者|たんとうしゃ}が{読|よ}み{直|なお}せるようにする。{閉幕|へいまく}の{一言|ひとこと}と{実務|じつむ}の{終了|しゅうりょう}は、{別々|べつべつ}に{確|たし}かめる{必要|ひつよう}があった。

watch.prompt: Optionally listen to an announcement or read a notice you already have. Separate the closing time from the means of contacting people; identify what work continues afterward.

recycling.reason: The newsletter/announcement unit naturally retrieves Hana’s 原稿 from the literary unit, but does not force grief, storm or fictional letter vocabulary into exhibit staffing. New formal headwords supplement reading study; scenes prioritise coherent peer planning.

exercises.prompt: What caused Ren to mix up the two incidents?
options: He read the two neighbouring articles together and assumed they concerned one person
Hana changed the quotation to the wrong date
The editor told Ren that the incidents concerned the same person
exercises.explain: Ren says he read the two articles consecutively; Hana clarifies 別の人.

exercises.prompt: Which conduct received the strong editorial criticism?
options: Correcting a date the next day with a reason
Inventing remarks from someone who had not been interviewed
Waiting for a speaker’s reply before filling the quote box
exercises.explain: Hana describes fabricated remarks printed as the person’s own words; the date error is a separate person’s incident.

exercises.prompt: What will Hana do before inserting the quotation?
options: Fill the box today using her own imagined words
Skip the arranged call because the date was corrected
Call tomorrow afternoon, then send the wording and wait for the speaker’s reply
exercises.explain: The arranged call is tomorrow afternoon; the wording follows it and the box stays empty pending a reply.

exercises.prompt: Complete the stated role judgement. It is conduct unworthy of an editor.
exercises.line: {編集者|へんしゅうしゃ}に＿＿{行為|こうい}だ。
exercises.explain: The frequent frame is role noun + にあるまじき + noun; the verb form is ある, not あった.

exercises.prompt: What does the editorial’s 編集者にあるまじき行為 express?
options: A claim that an editor physically cannot perform the act
Strong condemnation relative to an editor’s responsibilities
A polite routine invitation to edit the next issue
exercises.explain: まじき marks an unacceptable act against a standard, not factual impossibility.

exercises.prompt: Which use matches the distinction discussed here?
options: Call every corrected typo intentional fabrication
Use まじき as a warm greeting to a new volunteer
Quote the strong condemnation of fabricated remarks, while checking the separate date error on its own record
exercises.explain: The actual conduct and stated role establish the criticism’s scope; neighbouring articles do not merge their actors.

exercises.prompt: Which staffing plan does Hana state?
options: Two at the entrance and two guiding people in the hall
One person handling all reception and guidance
Two hundred volunteers at the entrance
exercises.explain: 入口に二人、会場の案内に二人 is the stated plan, not a universal staffing rule.

exercises.prompt: What makes the map the most troubling case in this draft?
options: The map includes a correct new date
The entrance and exit are reversed
Ren has already walked the corrected route
exercises.explain: Date and name errors come first; 案内図に至っては introduces the reversed entry and exit.

exercises.prompt: Which ending supplies an expected assessment after 二百人の会ともなると?
options: {私|わたし}は{受付|うけつけ}をしたい。
{受付|うけつけ}をしてください。
{受付|うけつけ}を{一人|ひとり}には{任|まか}せられない。
exercises.explain: The first judges what the larger gathering requires; the others are a direct wish and request.

exercises.prompt: Pick out the map as the worst case after the date and name errors.
exercises.line: {案内図|あんないず}＿＿、{入口|いりぐち}と{出口|でぐち}が{逆|ぎゃく}だった。
exercises.explain: に至っては singles out the extreme case. に至っても means even after reaching a stage, and the last phrase sets a reaching-time boundary.

exercises.prompt: Why does the writer separate the two people’s actions?
options: The date error is declared harmless to every visitor
A fabricated interview and a corrected date error require different factual accounts and responses
Both articles are about the same person and same action
exercises.explain: The first two paragraphs distinguish invented speech from an incorrect date; the next paragraph still asks who received the correction.

exercises.prompt: What does the correction box leave uncertain?
options: Whether a corrected date was ever published
Whether Ren wrote the fabricated remarks
Whether the people who saw the old date received a notice
exercises.explain: The writer says 古い日付を見た人に通知が届いたかは分からなかった. Publishing a repair is not the same as reaching earlier recipients.

exercises.prompt: What follows the on-site map correction?
options: Guides walk the same route to check it
The group publishes the unchanged previous-year plan
The editor fills the missing quotation from imagination
exercises.explain: The fifth paragraph first checks the entrance on site and corrects the diagram, then has the guides walk the route.

exercises.prompt: Which two closing times are different?
options: Viewing ends at five; applications stop at six
Applications for the next exhibition stop at five; current viewing ends at six
Both end at six and require advance applications
exercises.explain: Hana explicitly distinguishes 申し込みの受付は五時 and viewing until six without an application.

exercises.prompt: What does Hana say about this written notification?
options: Every recipient must return a stamped form
It is sent only to viewers who never applied to exhibit
It names the venue representative and does not require a seal
exercises.explain: The recipients are exhibition applicants; Hana says this notice does not need 捺印 and will name the representative.

exercises.prompt: What does をもって identify in 書面をもって申込者に通知します?
options: The formal means of notifying applicants in writing
A promise that each applicant has already replied
exercises.explain: 書面 names the means. The predicate 通知します does not assert a received reply or a time boundary.

exercises.prompt: Which time changed in the notice?
options: The application cutoff moved to six while viewing stayed at five
Exhibition viewing moved from five to six; the five-o’clock cutoff for the next exhibition stayed the same
Both moved from six to five
exercises.explain: The first paragraph names the former viewing end, adds one hour and explicitly says the application time did not change.

exercises.prompt: Why was written notice chosen for applicants?
options: So every applicant would have to return a stamped form
So nobody could ask the venue a question
So they could later reread when their exhibits could remain on display
exercises.explain: The second paragraph gives rereading the display deadline as the reason and denies a stamp-return procedure.

exercises.prompt: Why does Hana move her speech preparation away from the entrance?
options: Staying there would narrow visitors’ passage
The entrance diagram has never been repaired
She wants visitors to leave before five
exercises.explain: The fourth paragraph states that standing there would constrict the route; she prepares at another table.

exercises.prompt: Which work remains after the closing remarks?
options: Keep accepting applications after the exhibition closes
Record what happened, return borrowed items and leave notes for next year’s staff
Require every viewer to recite the closing phrase
exercises.explain: The final paragraph separates the end of the remarks from later practical work and gives these remaining actions.

grammar.title: Recognise an older negative, not every ぬ
grammar.formation: Modern negative ぬ: replace the ない of a verb negative with ぬ; する→せぬ, 来る→こぬ. In classical analysis this is negative ず in its noun-modifying form, after 未然形. Recognise fixed/formal uses; do not mechanically convert every modern predicate.
grammar.explanation: 知らぬ人 is someone one does not know; 思わぬ返事 is an unexpected reply. Modern remnants can also occur at the end of a marked written sentence. Older literature has a different completion auxiliary ぬ after 連用形: ending in ぬ alone never settles the meaning. This note teaches negative remnants, not all classical inflections. Standard everyday alternatives remain 知らない and 来ない.
grammar.example: 知らぬ人からの便りを、まだ開いていない。
grammar.translation: I haven't opened the letter from someone I don't know yet.

examples.ja: {知|し}らぬ{人|ひと}からの{便|たよ}りを、まだ{開|ひら}いていない。
examples.en: I haven't opened the letter from someone I don't know yet.

examples.ja: {思|おも}わぬ{返事|へんじ}が{届|とど}き、もう{一度|いちど}{読|よ}み{直|なお}した。
examples.en: An unexpected reply arrived, and I reread it.

examples.ja: 「{春|はる}はまだこぬ」の{来|こ}ぬは、ここでは「こぬ」と{読|よ}む。
examples.en: In “spring has not come yet,” 来ぬ is read konu here.

grammar.mistake: Do not read every written 来ぬ as こぬ or turn every ぬ into not. Classical completion 来ぬ may be きぬ; the base, reading and context matter.

grammar.title: Recognise a noun-modifying older negative
grammar.formation: Verb 未然形 + ざる + noun in classical-derived expressions; する→せざる, 来る→こざる. Recognise set/literary phrases such as 知らざる世界. Modern ない is the normal general negative.
grammar.explanation: ざる modifies the following noun in the uses taught here. 知らざる町 describes a town the speaker does not know. The older style is marked; it is not a friendlier everyday replacement for ない. Distinguish it from earlier ざるを得ない: that whole construction means having no choice, while 知らざる町 simply negates knowledge.
grammar.example: 書き手は「知らざる町」と記した。
grammar.translation: The writer wrote “a town unknown to me.”

examples.ja: {書|か}き{手|て}は「{知|し}らざる{町|まち}」と{記|しる}した。
examples.en: The writer wrote “a town unknown to me.”

examples.ja: {望|のぞ}まざる{変化|へんか}にも、{理由|りゆう}を{尋|たず}ねた。
examples.en: Even with an unwanted change, she asked the reason.

examples.ja: {忘|わす}れざる{一日|いちにち}は、{旅|たび}の{最初|さいしょ}の{日|ひ}だった。
examples.en: The day he would not forget was the first day of the trip.

grammar.mistake: Read the whole construction: ざる before a noun does not by itself mean must or have no choice. Do not attach it to the polite ます form.

grammar.title: Read a prohibition on a sign
grammar.formation: Dictionary verb + べからず. する/す + べからず; before a noun, べからざる in restricted established expressions such as 欠くべからざる + noun.
grammar.explanation: べからず gives an old-fashioned written prohibition in signs and rules. It does not report that the action has already happened or grant permission. People may quote or jokingly imitate it, but ordinary requests normally use familiar modern forms. 欠くべからざる in a noun phrase is a fixed way to call something indispensable; it is not a command forbidding that thing.
grammar.example: 古い立て札には「この橋を渡るべからず」とある。
grammar.translation: The old sign says, “Do not cross this bridge.”

examples.ja: {古|ふる}い{立|た}て{札|ふだ}には「この{橋|はし}を{渡|わた}るべからず」とある。
examples.en: The old sign says, “Do not cross this bridge.”

examples.ja: {庭|にわ}の{案内|あんない}には「{石碑|せきひ}に{登|のぼ}るべからず」と{記|しる}されている。
examples.en: The garden notice says, “Do not climb the stone monument.”

examples.ja: {案内係|あんないがかり}は、{混雑|こんざつ}した{会場|かいじょう}に{欠|か}くべからざる{存在|そんざい}だ。
examples.en: Guides are indispensable in a crowded venue.

grammar.mistake: Interpret the actual sign and its boundary. Do not treat an old exhibit label as proof of the current rule for the whole building; ask the venue. 欠くべからざる is a noun-modifying fixed expression.

grammar.title: Follow a literary comparison
grammar.formation: Noun + のごとし (predicate), のごとく (adverbial), のごとき + noun. Verb + がごとく/がごとき, often かのごとく/かのごとき. These are marked literary comparisons; learn the position in this unit.
grammar.explanation: ごとし ends a judgement, ごとく describes how an action or quality appears, and ごとき modifies a noun. The comparison does not establish a literal transformation. Direct person + ごとき can belittle someone, unlike an ordinary likeness phrase with の; interpret the tone and syntax rather than declaring every reference to a person insulting.
grammar.example: 水面は鏡のごとし、と彼女は書いた。
grammar.translation: She wrote that the water surface was like a mirror.

examples.ja: {水面|すいめん}は{鏡|かがみ}のごとし、と{彼女|かのじょ}は{書|か}いた。
examples.en: She wrote that the water surface was like a mirror.

examples.ja: {魚|さかな}のごとく{影|かげ}が{水面|すいめん}を{横切|よこぎ}った。
examples.en: A shadow crossed the water surface like a fish.

examples.ja: {鏡|かがみ}のごとき{水面|すいめん}に、{雲|くも}が{映|うつ}った。
examples.en: Clouds appeared on the mirrorlike water surface.

grammar.mistake: Use ごとき before a noun and ごとく to modify the action in these frames. A simile is not a literal identity; direct belittling 人+ごとき needs context.

grammar.title: Spot the separate classical completion ぬ
grammar.formation: Classical completion: verb 連用形 + ぬ (conclusive), not negative 未然形 + ぬ. 来る has classical き + ぬ for completion versus こ + ぬ for negative. This unit recognises a few labelled original literary phrases only.
grammar.explanation: 雨やみぬ means the rain has stopped in the labelled literary narration; 雨やまぬ means it does not stop in the contrasting negative phrase. 春きぬ describes spring arriving; 春はまだこぬ says it has not come yet. These supplied readings reveal the different bases. Other older spellings may require a reference and wider context. Do not infer a tense from the final ぬ alone or claim this note teaches full classical grammar.
grammar.example: 原稿の「雨やみぬ」は、雨が止んだという文語の表現だ。
grammar.translation: The draft’s “ame yaminu” is literary wording saying the rain stopped.

examples.ja: {原稿|げんこう}の「{雨|あめ}やみぬ」は、{雨|あめ}が{止|や}んだという{文語|ぶんご}の{表現|ひょうげん}だ。
examples.en: The draft’s “ame yaminu” is literary wording saying the rain stopped.

examples.ja: 「はるきぬ」と{書|か}き、{春|はる}が{来|き}た{場面|ばめん}を{描|えが}いた。
examples.en: She wrote “haru kinu” to describe spring having arrived.

examples.ja: 「{雨|あめ}やまぬ{夜|よる}」のやまぬは、{雨|あめ}が{止|や}まないという{否定|ひてい}だ。
examples.en: Yamanu in “a night when the rain does not stop” is negative.

grammar.mistake: The contrast is between different auxiliaries/bases, not merely polite versus casual or a long versus short vowel. If only an ambiguous old spelling is given, consult its context and reading.

grammar: an older negative used in a quoted text
an old-fashioned prohibition on an actual sign
a literary simile and its real referent
the different bases before negative and completion ぬ
watch.prompt: Optionally read a text you already have. Keep original wording separate from a modern paraphrase; use its reading/context to identify an older ending, and note when a literary comparison is not literal.

recycling.reason: The original-draft revision retrieves 原稿 from N1 unit 1 without forcing newsletter misconduct or exhibition staffing into borrowed-book reading and a river story. Natural conversation and actual quoted remnants take priority over a mechanical percentage.

exercises.prompt: What does Hana say 思わぬ便り means here?
options: A letter the writer had not expected
A letter written without any thoughts
Proof that the sender is a bad person
exercises.explain: Hana supplies 思いがけない. Neither the phrase nor the scene calls the sender bad.

exercises.prompt: Does Hana already know who sent the letter from the town?
options: No; the name has not appeared yet
Yes; a professor is explicitly named
exercises.explain: 名前が出てない is explicit. The next page may reveal the sender, but that has not happened.

exercises.prompt: How will they keep the notes?
options: Erase the original and replace it with a guessed sender
Write the translation directly into the borrowed book
Separate the original wording and modern-language notes
exercises.explain: 別々にしておこう and separate paper are stated. The book is borrowed.

exercises.prompt: Form the older negative of する by the special form taught here.
exercises.line: まだ{確認|かくにん}＿＿。
exercises.explain: The negative remnant is せぬ. しぬ is not this negative formation; するぬ does not attach to the negative base.

exercises.prompt: What does 知らざる町 describe in the supplied passage?
options: A town the writer has no choice but to move to
A town the writer does not know
exercises.explain: ざる modifies 町. The full ざるを得ない construction and claims about danger are absent.

exercises.prompt: Choose the older negative that modifies 町: a town one does not know.
exercises.line: ＿＿{町|まち}から{便|たよ}りが{届|とど}いた。
exercises.explain: 知ら is the negative base; ざる modifies the following noun. The others use polite/past forms rather than this base.

exercises.prompt: How do they establish that the bridge is currently closed?
options: They find a current no-entry notice before the bridge and learn it is under repair
They assume every bridge is closed because of the displayed old sign
They hear that the bridge has already reopened
exercises.explain: The new notice and repair state establish the current closure; the display alone did not.

exercises.prompt: What does reception tell Ren?
options: The bridge is safe to cross despite the repair notice
They can reach the garden through the covered passage
They can photograph inside the exhibition room
exercises.explain: 回廊から行ける is reported. Photos are allowed in the garden but not the exhibition room.

exercises.prompt: A sign says この橋を渡るべからず. What instruction does it give?
options: Please cross before taking a photo
exercises.explain: べからず marks prohibition in the stated sign, not past action or an invitation.

exercises.prompt: What does 案内係は欠くべからざる存在だ express in a crowded venue?
options: The guides are forbidden to exist
exercises.explain: 欠くべからざる before 存在 is the established indispensable expression, not a ban on guides.

exercises.prompt: Whose loan slip was found when the writer returned the book?
options: The writer’s; they keep it as their own translation
A previous borrower’s; the writer gives it to the staff member
exercises.explain: The fifth paragraph distinguishes the previous borrower’s loan slip from the narrator’s annotation paper.

exercises.prompt: Which pair of permissions is actually established?
options: Cross the repaired bridge; photograph inside the exhibition room
Climb the monument; take photos anywhere
Use the covered passage to the garden; take photos in the garden only
exercises.explain: Reception supplies the path; the following paragraph explicitly restricts photography to the garden.

exercises.prompt: What does Hana correct about her character’s action?
options: The character starts to throw the letter but does not throw it
The character throws the letter and receives a reply immediately
The character never takes the letter out
exercises.explain: Hana retracts 投げます and says 投げようとして、結局、投げません.

exercises.prompt: Use the literary comparison before the noun 水面 in this taught frame.
exercises.line: {鏡|かがみ}の＿＿{水面|すいめん}に、{雲|くも}が{映|うつ}った。
exercises.explain: ごとき modifies 水面; ごとく is adverbial and ごとし is the predicate form.

exercises.prompt: The labelled literary draft says 雨やみぬ. How does it differ from 雨やまぬ?
options: Both necessarily mean it does not stop
The difference is only a polite versus casual tone
やみ + completion ぬ says it stopped; やま + negative ぬ says it does not stop
exercises.explain: The supplied different bases distinguish completion and negative. Ending in ぬ alone is not enough.

exercises.prompt: What makes the narrator bring her hand back?
options: She sees her grip reflected and questions why she holds the letter so tightly
A fish takes the letter from her hand
The sender calls and demands a reply
exercises.explain: The third paragraph gives the reflection and her question; no fish or call intervenes.

exercises.prompt: What caused the fishlike shadow?
options: A train moving over the bridge
A visitor crossing the closed bridge from the other passage
exercises.explain: The fourth paragraph explicitly identifies a train’s shadow; ごとく is a comparison.

exercises.prompt: Which status is explicit when the narrator gets home?
options: The recipient has already read and answered the reply
She has phoned the recipient and sealed the envelope
She makes a reply draft and plans to reread it next morning before sending
exercises.explain: The last paragraph states a draft, no phone call and an unsealed envelope. Receiving a reply is not established.

exercises.prompt: The reference supplies 春きぬ for completion and 春はまだこぬ for negative. Which account is accurate?
options: The readings and verb bases distinguish arrival from not yet arriving
Every spelling 来ぬ must always be read こぬ and be negative
Both forms are ordinary polite requests to bring spring
exercises.explain: The supplied classical き versus negative こ makes the distinction. An ambiguous spelling needs context/reference.

exercises.prompt: Why does the draft move the fishlike shadow to after the hand movement?
options: To claim the train physically becomes a fish
To show that she stops before the train shadow passes, rather than implying she drops the letter in surprise
To establish that the sender has already replied
exercises.explain: The prose separates the action and later shadow. The comparison neither changes the train’s identity nor establishes a received reply.

lessons.title: Read the concession and the conclusion
lessons.description: Read the notice and quoted editorial without assuming permanent approval.
lessons.canDo: Separate a concession from the final recommendation.

lessons.canDo: Preserve scope and practical conditions when summarising an argument.

lessons.title: A smaller proposal is still a proposal

grammar.title: Acknowledge a point; keep the qualification
grammar.formation: Plain verb/i-adjective + とはいえ; noun/na-adjective (だ) + とはいえ. It can also begin a sentence referring to the previous statement.
grammar.explanation: Accept a fact or description, then add a judgement or outcome that the first part alone would not lead you to expect. The qualification matters to the conclusion. It does not necessarily mean the first fact was false.
grammar.example: 夜の利用時間が増えるとはいえ、職員の休憩も確保しなければならない。
grammar.translation: Even though evening access will increase, staff breaks must also be secured.

examples.ja: {夜|よる}の{利用時間|りようじかん}が{増|ふ}えるとはいえ、{職員|しょくいん}の{休憩|きゅうけい}も{確保|かくほ}しなければならない。
examples.en: Even though evening access will increase, staff breaks must also be secured.

examples.ja: {予算|よさん}は{少|すこ}ない。とはいえ、{三週間|さんしゅうかん}の{試行|しこう}は{可能|かのう}だ。
examples.en: The budget is small. Still, a three-week trial is possible.

examples.ja: {便利|べんり}だとはいえ、{予約|よやく}だけでは{借|か}りられない{本|ほん}もある。
examples.en: Even though it is convenient, some books cannot be borrowed through a reservation alone.

grammar.mistake: Do not translate every concession as a rejection of the acknowledged fact. Several connectors overlap; follow the whole argument.

grammar.title: A formal concession does not erase the limit
grammar.formation: Plain statement + といえども. A noun can directly precede it; noun/na-adjective predicates can include だ/である in a fuller clause.
grammar.explanation: A marked formal concession can take a noteworthy or extreme case and deny the expected consequence. Recognition in editorials and quoted statements is the focus; friends normally use plainer wording outside quotation.
grammar.example: 館長といえども、一人で開館時間を決められるわけではない。
grammar.translation: Even the library director cannot decide opening hours alone.

examples.ja: {館長|かんちょう}といえども、{一人|ひとり}で{開館時間|かいかんじかん}を{決|き}められるわけではない。
examples.en: Even the library director cannot decide opening hours alone.

examples.ja: たとえ{短|みじか}い{試行|しこう}といえども、{職員|しょくいん}の{勤務時間|きんむじかん}を{確認|かくにん}する{必要|ひつよう}がある。
examples.en: Even a short trial requires checking staff working hours.

examples.ja: {予算|よさん}が{増|ふ}えたといえども、{使|つか}い{道|みち}が{全|すべ}て{決|き}まったわけではない。
examples.en: Even though the budget increased, not all of its uses have been decided.

grammar.mistake: This form is not a causal because. Do not make とはいえ and といえども rivals in a gap when both fit; assess register or meaning with context.

grammar.title: A stated claim meets a practical qualification
grammar.formation: Plain statement + とはいうものの; noun/na-adjective predicates may include だ. Sentence-initial use can refer back to a stated claim.
grammar.explanation: Acknowledge something said, proposed or commonly described, then qualify how it works in practice. Here the notice and an actual proposal supply that claim. This can overlap with とはいえ; no absolute quoted-versus-unquoted ban is taught.
grammar.example: 夜間利用を認めるとはいうものの、今は金曜日だけの試行だ。
grammar.translation: Although evening use is being allowed, for now the trial is only on Fridays.

examples.ja: {夜間|やかん}{利用|りよう}を{認|みと}めるとはいうものの、{今|いま}は{金曜日|きんようび}だけの{試行|しこう}だ。
examples.en: Although evening use is being allowed, for now the trial is only on Fridays.

examples.ja: {延長|えんちょう}は{好評|こうひょう}だとはいうものの、{毎晩|まいばん}{続|つづ}ける{人件費|じんけんひ}はまだ{計算|けいさん}していない。
examples.en: Although the extension is well received, we haven't calculated the personnel cost of continuing every evening.

examples.ja: {新|あたら}しい{書架|しょか}を{入|い}れるという{案|あん}がある。とはいうものの、{置|お}く{場所|ばしょ}はまだ{決|き}まっていない。
examples.en: There's a proposal to add a new book stack. That said, its location hasn't been decided yet.

grammar.mistake: Do not infer permanent approval from a generally worded claim; retain its actual timing and conditions. The final clause is not automatically total opposition.

grammar.title: An unattained extent, then a lesser one
grammar.formation: Verb negative form + までも; noun/na-adjective + ではないまでも is also recognised.
grammar.explanation: A greater or extreme extent is not asserted/reached, but a lesser extent remains: not every evening, but selected evenings; not eliminating a problem, but reducing it. Both desirable and undesirable scales occur. This is not doing nothing, and it differs from までもない (no need).
grammar.example: 毎晩開けられないまでも、週に一度は利用できるようにしたい。
grammar.translation: Even if we can't open every evening, we'd like to make it available once a week.

examples.ja: {毎晩|まいばん}{開|あ}けられないまでも、{週|しゅう}に{一度|いちど}は{利用|りよう}できるようにしたい。
examples.en: Even if we can't open every evening, we'd like to make it available once a week.

examples.ja: {待|ま}ち{時間|じかん}をなくせないまでも、{短|みじか}くする{工夫|くふう}はできる。
examples.en: Even if we can't eliminate the wait, we can find ways to shorten it.

examples.ja: {十分|じゅうぶん}な{予算|よさん}ではないまでも、{今月|こんげつ}の{試行|しこう}に{必要|ひつよう}な{額|がく}はある。
examples.en: Even if the budget isn't ample, we have the amount needed for this month's trial.

grammar.mistake: Keep the scale meaningful. In 開けられないまでも, ない belongs to the verb negative; it does not mean there is no need to open.
